---
title: 2-of-3 Shamir backup
description: Split your recovery secret so no single lost device can lock you out.
---

Obsign backs up your recovery secret using **Shamir's Secret Sharing**, split
2-of-3: three shares are created, and any **two** of them reconstruct the
secret. No single share reveals anything on its own.

## Why 2-of-3

- **Lose one share** (a stolen phone, a wiped laptop) and you can still recover
  with the remaining two.
- **A single leaked share is useless.** One share alone cannot reconstruct
  anything.

The split balances the two ways a backup can fail: one lost device locking you
out forever, and one leaked secret being game over.

## Where the three shares live

Backup is built into creating your identity; there is no separate menu option
to turn it on. Right after your identity is created, Obsign shows the
**Back up your recovery key** step, and the three shares already have their
homes:

- **Share 1 of 3** is saved automatically to your device's **Keychain** and
  marked for **iCloud Keychain** sync, so it can reach your other Apple
  devices. Obsign can confirm it wrote the share; only Apple can deliver it,
  and with iCloud Keychain switched off it stays on this device.
- **Share 2 of 3** is held in your **server's escrow**.
- **Share 3 of 3** is **yours to save**. Obsign shows it as a numbered
  **word phrase** (with a QR form for machines) and a Copy button; keep it
  somewhere durable.

The split happens **on your device**: your phone generates the recovery secret
and hands the server Share 2 and nothing else. No server database, and no
backup of one, can ever reconstruct your secret.

You confirm you've saved Share 3 before you can continue. Obsign already holds
two shares for you (iCloud and your server), so saving Share 3 anywhere
independent of your phone gives you a second, self-controlled path back in.

:::tip[Good homes for Share 3]
Save it to a password manager (1Password, Bitwarden, …), print it and store it
somewhere safe, or write it down and keep it **separate from your device**. Do
not leave it only on the phone that also holds Share 1.
:::

## Recovering with two shares

Lost the phone entirely? On a new device, choose **I lost access to my wallet**
on Obsign's first screen. Any two of your three shares bring the identity back:

- **The common path.** Share 1 loads automatically if iCloud Keychain carried
  it to the new device, and Obsign asks your server to release its escrowed
  Share 2. The release is slow on purpose: a single-use code is emailed to your
  account address, and after you enter it the share stays **pending for a delay
  window** before it can be collected. The wait is shown in the app, and a
  pending release can be cancelled, so a stolen mailbox alone cannot quietly
  drain your escrow.
- **The sovereign path.** Share 1 plus the Share 3 word phrase you saved. This
  path reconstructs everything locally and asks your server for nothing.
- **Share 2 + Share 3.** The escrowed share plus your word phrase. This works
  with no Share 1 at all, which is why saving Share 3 is not optional.

:::caution[When Share 1 won't be waiting for you]
Obsign marks Share 1 for iCloud Keychain sync, but it cannot see whether Apple
delivered it. Two cases leave a new device without it:

- **iCloud Keychain is switched off** on your Apple account. Turning it on
  later lets the share sync with no further action in Obsign, but only from a
  device that still holds it.
- **The identity was set up by an older version of Obsign**, which kept Share 1
  on a single device. Updating and opening the app on a device that still holds
  that share fixes it from then on. If that device is already gone, nothing can
  reach back and repair it; that identity stays on Share 2 + Share 3 for good.

In both cases your saved Share 3 is the way back in.
:::

Obsign verifies the reconstructed key against your identity's public record
before anything is allowed to sign, and tells you in plain words if a share is
corrupted or belongs to an older backup generation.

Recovery always ends with a **rotation**: the recovered identity gets a fresh
recovery secret and a fresh set of three shares, so every share the lost device
ever touched is void. Saving the new Share 3 is part of finishing, and the
rotation resumes where it left off if it's interrupted.

:::note[Created your identity a while ago?]
Identities created before on-device recovery keys show a calm **Add a recovery
key** prompt on the home screen. Accepting it re-runs the split with your
device doing the generating (the server receives only Share 2) and walks you
through saving a new Share 3. Every step is additive and resumable; your device
key never moves, so an interrupted upgrade never leaves you worse off than
before.
:::

Your other safety net is unchanged: because your identity key sits on your
device as the highest-priority key, you can
[override an unexpected change](/user/recovery/) within a 72-hour window
without reassembling any shares.

:::note[This page describes did:plc identities]
The 2-of-3 split backs the recovery key of a **did:plc** identity — the
default. A
[did:web identity](/user/getting-started/#advanced-anchor-your-identity-to-a-domain-you-own-didweb)
carries no shares and no escrow; its recovery model is control of its domain.
:::

---
title: Signing in to apps
description: Approve sign-in to a third-party ATProtocol app with your wallet — no password.
---

Obsign identities don't have a password. The keys that prove who you are live
on your device, so there's nothing for an app to check against a server.
Instead, you approve each sign-in in the wallet: your device key does the
proving, confirmed with Face ID or Touch ID, and no password is ever involved.

## How it works

When you sign in to an ATProtocol app with an Obsign identity, the app sends
you to your server's sign-in page. Instead of a password box, that page shows
three ways to hand the request to your wallet:

- a short **typed code**,
- a **QR code**, and
- an **Open in Obsign** link (when the app is on the same phone as your
  wallet).

Bring the request into Obsign by any one of them. The wallet then shows you
exactly what you're about to approve:

- the **app** asking to sign in,
- the **origin** it's running on,
- the identity you'd sign in **as**, and
- the **permissions** it's requesting.

Check that preview, drop any permissions you don't want to grant, and confirm
with Face ID or Touch ID. That's the sign-in. The app's page notices the
approval and finishes on its own.

### Bring the request in three ways

**Typed code.** Read the short code off the sign-in page and enter it in
Obsign. This always works: no camera, no second device, and it reads cleanly
for screen readers. It's the fallback the other two fall back to.

**QR code.** Point the phone camera at the QR beside the code. Best when the
app is on a different screen from your wallet — a laptop, say — because you
can't scan your own phone's screen.

**Open in Obsign.** When the app and the wallet are on the same phone, tap the
link and it opens Obsign straight to the approval. No typing, no scanning.

### Or let the sign-in come to you

If your server supports push notifications and you've allowed them, the wallet
can also prompt you the moment a sign-in is requested for your account. Tapping
the notification opens the same approval screen. On this path the sign-in page
also shows a **two-digit number**, and the wallet asks you to type it before it
will approve. That number is the proof you're actually looking at the sign-in
you're approving, so a stray prompt can't be granted with a reflexive tap.

## Why this is safe

The QR, the handoff link, and the push notification carry only a request id —
never the app name, origin, or permissions. Obsign takes that id and fetches
the real details **from your own server**, then shows you those. A doctored QR
can't trick you into approving something other than what your server actually
recorded: what you see in the preview is the source of truth, not what the
code claimed.

A few more guarantees hold on every path:

- **Your key approves, not a session.** The confirmation is a signature from
  your device key, checked against your identity's authoritative rotation
  keys, the same keys that anchor the identity itself. Approving a login is
  something only the holder of the identity can do.
- **One use, then it's spent.** Each request works once and expires in about
  five minutes.
- **No replay, no scope creep.** The signature is bound to that specific
  request and to the exact set of permissions you granted. It can't be
  replayed onto a different sign-in or a wider set of permissions.
- **Approvals and denials are both recorded.** If you deny a request, that
  ends it, and the decision is written to your identity's audit trail either
  way.

:::note[Reducing what you grant]
The permission checkboxes live in the wallet, not on the web page — the wallet
is the trusted surface for this decision. Uncheck anything the app asked for
that you don't want to hand over before you confirm; the app only gets what
you approved.
:::

---
title: Backing up your content
description: Keep your own verified copy of your posts and media in iCloud — the one backup that survives your server failing.
---

Your server holds two kinds of thing for you: your **posts** (the records:
every post, like, follow, and profile edit) and your **media** (the photos and
video attached to them, plus your avatar and banner). Obsign can keep a second
copy of both, held by **you** in your own iCloud Drive, so a server that loses
them, or goes away entirely, isn't the end of the story.

Both backups are opt-in, per identity, and live side by side on the
**Media backup** screen (reached from an identity's detail view).

:::note[This is a different backup from your recovery key]
The [2-of-3 Shamir backup](/user/backup/) protects the **key that proves who
you are** — your way back in if you lose your phone. This page is about backing
up **your content**. One protects access, the other protects content. You want
both.
:::

## Why hold your own copy

Your server already backs its data up off-box (operators can read how in
[Backups & restore](/operator/backups/)). That protects you if a *file*
goes bad. It does not protect you if the *server itself* goes away: a host
that shuts down, a volume lost with no restore point, an operator you no
longer trust.

A backup you hold is the layer underneath all of that. It lives in your iCloud
Drive, so it survives the server entirely. And because your posts reference
media by **content address** — a hash of the bytes themselves — your copy is
either exactly the file the post points at or it isn't. There is no "close
enough."

## Backing up your media

Open an identity and choose **Back up media**. The backup is:

- **Opt-in, per identity.** Nothing is copied anywhere until you ask, and each
  identity is backed up on its own.
- **Incremental.** The first run copies everything; later runs only fetch
  what's new, so keeping it current is cheap.
- **Verified as it goes.** Every file is checked against its content address
  before it's written to the mirror, so a corrupted download is never stored
  as if it were good.

The current mirror size is always shown, and the copy is a normal folder you
can see in the **Files** app. Nothing hidden, nothing you can't inspect.

## Keeping it fresh

Media you post keeps arriving after the first backup, so Obsign tops the
mirror up on its own. On iOS a scheduled background task refreshes each
opted-in identity's mirror without you opening the app, running the same
incremental, content-verified pass as **Back up now**. A photo posted days ago
doesn't sit unprotected until the next time you happen to launch Obsign, and
each identity is handled independently, so one account's failure never stops
the others.

You stay in control of when that happens. A **Media backup** section in
Settings lets you:

- turn background backups **off** entirely (leaving only the manual **Back up
  now**),
- restrict them to **while charging**, or
- **skip cellular data**, so top-ups wait for Wi-Fi.

## Restoring to your server

If your server loses the originals, open the identity and choose **Restore to
server**. Obsign uploads your mirrored files back **byte-for-byte**. Media is
content-addressed, so the restored files carry the same addresses they had
before, and every post keeps pointing at the same media. Nothing in your posts
is rewritten.

iOS sometimes offloads files from a full device to save space, leaving only a
placeholder. A restore handles that for you: when a backed-up file isn't
actually on the phone, Obsign asks iCloud to download it, waits for it to
arrive (within a time limit), verifies it still matches its content address,
and uploads it. A restore on a device where most of the mirror has been
evicted just works, instead of handing you a list of files to fetch by hand.
The summary tells you how many files were pulled from iCloud first, so a
slower restore explains itself. A file that's genuinely gone, with no iCloud
copy left to download, is reported on its own, and the restore continues past
it.

## During a migration

Your media backup also protects a **move**. When you
[migrate your identity](/user/migration/) away from a server that has already
lost some of your media, that media would normally be left behind. If you've
backed it up, Obsign falls back to your own copy: it verifies the backed-up
file still matches its content address and uploads *that* to your new server.
The substitution is exact, so a file your old server dropped shrinks the
move's loss list — and ideally empties it — instead of forcing you to skip it.

## Backing up your posts

Your **posts** — the records themselves — are the one part of your account
that otherwise lives only on your server. The same **Media backup** screen has
a **Back up your posts** section that mirrors a full snapshot of your
repository into your iCloud Drive.

- **A snapshot, not a stream.** Each backup captures your whole repository as
  it stands, so the copy you hold is always a complete, self-contained record
  rather than a pile of fragments.
- **Integrity-checked before it's kept.** A snapshot is verified before it
  replaces the last one. If a freshly fetched copy fails the check, the
  previous good snapshot is left untouched; you are never left holding a
  corrupt backup.
- **Yours to keep and to move.** The snapshot is a standard repository export
  you can hold, inspect, and carry to another server, so the record of what
  you've written stays with you no matter what happens to the server that
  hosted it.

Together with your media backup, this means your whole presence — what you
wrote and the images you attached — has a copy that you control.

13	Linear team is **MM** ("Mal's Machinations"), project **ezpds**. Two access paths from Claude Code:
14	
15	- **Writes** (status changes, comments, create/update issues): there are usually **two** Linear MCP servers listed. `plugin:linear:linear` is the OAuth one and is often unauthorized (a non-interactive session cannot fix that). A **second, already-authorized** Linear server appears under an opaque UUID name (e.g. `mcp__202234c8-43b0-47f5-be47-37bc8d2deb1b__save_issue`) — its tools are deferred, so `ToolSearch` for `linear issue create save project` to load them. **Check for the UUID server before reporting Linear writes as unavailable.** `save_issue(id:"MM-98", state:"Done")` and `save_comment(issueId:"MM-98", body:...)` take identifiers directly; `state` accepts a name/type/ID.
16	- **Reads**: `LINEAR_API_KEY` is in `.env.local` (gitignored). `set -a; source .env.local; set +a` then POST GraphQL to `https://api.linear.app/graphql` with header `Authorization: $LINEAR_API_KEY`. Good for wave/label scans.
17	
18	**The GitHub integration already does the PR bookkeeping.** Opening a PR whose title/branch names the issue (e.g. `MM-472`) auto-attaches it to the issue AND auto-moves the state — observed 2026-07-25: MM-472 went `Done` → back to `In Review` on its own the moment a second PR (#439) opened against it. So after `gh pr create`, **check the issue state before setting it** — a redundant `save_issue(state:…)` is usually unnecessary, and blindly forcing a state can undo what the integration correctly did.
19	
20	**Gotchas:**
21	- **A `502 upstream_unavailable` from `save_issue` can be a FALSE failure — the write lands anyway.** Observed 2026-07-27: a create returned `{"error":"upstream_unavailable","status":502}`, the naive retry succeeded, and both issues existed (MM-483 from the "failed" call, MM-484 from the retry). **Never blind-retry a Linear write after a 5xx** — first `list_issues` (or `get_issue` on the next identifier in sequence) to check whether it already landed. A tell-tale sign after the fact is an identifier gap: a retry that returns MM-N+2 when you expected MM-N+1 means N+1 is your duplicate. Clean up with `save_issue(id: <dup>, duplicateOf: <original>)`, which sets status `Duplicate`; note that still counts against the 250-issue free-plan cap until archived.
22	- The `linear_wave_status` / `linear_list_issues` / `linear_update_issue` tools named in AGENTS.md are **Pi** extension tools (`.pi/extensions/linear/index.ts`), NOT available to Claude Code. Don't try to call them — replicate their GraphQL instead, or use the MCP.
23	- **Writes via Bash** (curl/python hitting the Linear API) are **hard-blocked** by the auto-mode classifier as external-system writes, even with user authorization. Writes must go through the authenticated MCP.
24	- zsh mangles `!` inside heredoc'd GraphQL (`String!` → `String\!`); inline values or put the query in a file written via the Write tool.
25	- The exhaustive `issues(first: 250)` wave-status scan can return HTTP 500; page smaller or filter by label (e.g. `labels: { name: { eq: "Wave 4: Repo + Blobs" } }`).
26	- **Wave labels are team-scoped to MM, not workspace-level.** `list_issue_labels` with NO `team` arg returns an incomplete set (only a few labels) — call it with `team:"MM"` to see the full wave list. Its `name:` filter is **exact-match, not substring** (`name:"Wave"` returns zero labels); omit it and scan the full list instead. Also: the notification-relay epic (MM-419/420/423/443, 2026-07) has **no wave label** — don't force one of the v0.1 waves onto notify issues. Their real names carry a suffix: `Wave 0: Scaffolding`, `Wave 1: Running Server`, `Wave 2: Auth`, `Wave 3: Identity` AND `Wave 3: Key Sovereignty` (two Wave-3 labels), `Wave 4: Repo + Blobs`, `Wave 5: Federation`, `Wave 6: App Proxy`, `Wave 7: Hardening`, `Wave 8: auth.md`. `save_issue(labels:[...])` matches on the **exact full name** — `labels:["Wave 7"]` silently no-ops (returns `labels:[]`); use `"Wave 7: Hardening"`.

input.description:
Bring the two runaway AGENTS.md files down to the map-not-territory register defined in [docs/writing-style.md](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/blob/main/docs/writing-style.md) (PR #496): an entry is a few lines — what the module is, the one or two facts an agent needs before opening it, and a pointer to the module doc. Detail lives in exactly one home, nearest the code.

**Scope:**
- `crates/pds/AGENTS.md` (~15k words) — the routes table's paragraph-length cells are the bulk; also the `firehose/`, `identity/`, `auth/`, `db/` narrative sections.
- `apps/identity-wallet/AGENTS.md` (~10k words) — the Exposes/Guarantees/Invariants lists restate module docs and serde contracts at length.

1. Per file/section, first verify whether the detail already exists in the module doc. Where it does (the common case — see the `crawler.rs`/`relay_status.rs` pilot), the diet is pure dedup.
2. Where AGENTS.md is the *only* home of a fact, move it INTO the module doc first, then shrink the entry to a pointer. Never delete a fact that has no other home.
3. Per-file (or per-section) PRs so each diff is reviewable; run `just ticket-ref-check` + `just docs-check` per PR.

Expected 60–70% reduction with zero information loss. This also cuts the context these files consume when auto-loaded into every agent session touching the crate.

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# Require a changelog fragment *added by the change itself* when a PR changes a shipped
3	# surface (fragments already sitting in changelog.d/ from other work don't satisfy it).
4	# CHANGELOG_BASE_REF is set to the PR base SHA in CI; an explicit first argument is
5	# convenient for local checks. With neither, fragment validity is still checked but
6	# presence is not required because there is no trustworthy comparison range.
7	set -euo pipefail
8	
9	cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
10	
11	base_ref="${1:-${CHANGELOG_BASE_REF:-}}"
12	fragment_dir="changelog.d"
13	fragment_re='^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*\.(added|changed|fixed|removed|security)\.md$'
14	
15	fail=0
16	fragment_count=0
17	while IFS= read -r fragment; do
18	  name="${fragment##*/}"
19	  if ! [[ "$name" =~ $fragment_re ]]; then
20	    echo "✗ invalid changelog fragment '$fragment' — expected <id>.<added|changed|fixed|removed|security>.md" >&2
21	    fail=1
22	    continue
23	  fi
24	  if ! grep -q '[^[:space:]]' "$fragment"; then
25	    echo "✗ changelog fragment '$fragment' is empty" >&2
26	    fail=1
27	    continue
28	  fi
29	  fragment_count=$((fragment_count + 1))
30	done < <(find "$fragment_dir" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.md' ! -name README.md | sort)
31	
32	if [ "$fail" -ne 0 ]; then
33	  exit 1
34	fi
35	
36	if [ -z "$base_ref" ]; then
37	  echo "✓ $fragment_count valid changelog fragment(s); no base ref supplied, so presence was not evaluated"
38	  exit 0
39	fi
40	
41	if ! git rev-parse --verify "${base_ref}^{commit}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
42	  echo "✗ changelog base ref '$base_ref' is not available — fetch the PR base before running this check" >&2
43	  exit 1
44	fi
45	
46	# Presence must be satisfied by fragments this change ADDS, not by whatever happens to be
47	# sitting in changelog.d/ already — a pre-existing fragment from an unmerged sibling or an
48	# unconsumed earlier PR would otherwise let a fragment-less shipped change slide through.
49	added_fragment_count=0
50	while IFS= read -r fragment; do
51	  name="${fragment##*/}"
52	  if [[ "$name" =~ $fragment_re ]]; then
53	    added_fragment_count=$((added_fragment_count + 1))
54	  fi
55	done < <(git diff --name-only --diff-filter=A "${base_ref}...HEAD" -- "$fragment_dir")
56	
57	changed_files="$(git diff --name-only "${base_ref}...HEAD")"
58	shipped_files="$(printf '%s\n' "$changed_files" | awk '
59	  /(^|\/)AGENTS\.md$/ { next }
60	  # The browser test harness sits under an apps/*/src/ path but is developer tooling, which
61	  # this gate deliberately does not cover (see changelog.d/README.md). It is not merely
62	  # unused in production — it is double-gated on `import.meta.env.DEV && VITE_HARNESS` and
63	  # proven absent from the build by `pnpm check:harness-absence`, so no harness change can
64	  # reach a user and none has a release note to write. Without this skip the broad
65	  # apps/*/src/ rule below claims it, and every fixture fix has to invent a user-facing
66	  # sentence about a screenshot scenario.
67	  /^apps\/[^\/]+\/src\/lib\/harness\// { next }
68	  /^Cargo\.toml$/ || /^Cargo\.lock$/ || /^Dockerfile$/ || /^railway\.toml$/ { print; next }
69	  /^nix\/module\.nix$/ { print; next }
70	  /^sites\/marketing\// { print; next }
71	  /^crates\/[^\/]+\/src\// || /^crates\/pds\/assets\// { print; next }
72	  # The notification relay ships its own image and Railway config, the same shipped-surface
73	  # status the repo-root and sidecar deploy files already carry.
74	  /^crates\/notify-relay\/(Dockerfile|docker-entrypoint\.sh|railway\.toml)$/ { print; next }
75	  /^apps\/[^\/]+\/src\// || /^apps\/[^\/]+\/src-tauri\/src\// { print; next }
76	  /^apps\/[^\/]+\/static\// || /^apps\/[^\/]+\/tauri\.conf\.json$/ { print; next }
77	  /^tools\/mcp\/src\// { print; next }
78	  /^tools\/mcp-sidecar\/src\// || /^tools\/mcp-sidecar\/Dockerfile$/ || /^tools\/mcp-sidecar\/railway\.toml$/ { print; next }
79	')"
80	
81	# A release roll-up (`just set-version`) legitimately consumes every fragment while it bumps
82	# the workspace version and touches Cargo.toml/Cargo.lock — so it changes shipped surfaces
83	# yet cannot carry a fragment. Recognize that exact shape (the [workspace.package] version
84	# line changed AND a new dated release heading was added to CHANGELOG.md) and waive the
85	# presence requirement. Both signals are required, so a plain CHANGELOG.md edit can never
86	# be used to smuggle a real feature past the gate.
87	is_release_rollup() {
88	  git diff "${base_ref}...HEAD" -- Cargo.toml \
89	    | grep -qE '^\+version = "[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+"$' || return 1
90	  git diff "${base_ref}...HEAD" -- CHANGELOG.md \
91	    | grep -qE '^\+## \[[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\] - [0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$' || return 1
92	}
93	
94	if [ -n "$shipped_files" ] && [ "$added_fragment_count" -eq 0 ]; then
95	  if is_release_rollup; then
96	    echo "✓ release roll-up detected (workspace version bump + new CHANGELOG.md section); fragment presence not required"
97	    exit 0
98	  fi
99	  echo "✗ this change touches shipped surfaces but adds no changelog.d/<id>.<type>.md fragment:" >&2
100	  while IFS= read -r shipped_file; do
101	    printf '  %s\n' "$shipped_file" >&2
102	  done <<< "$shipped_files"
103	  echo "  Pre-existing fragments in changelog.d/ don't count — the fragment must be added by this change." >&2
104	  echo "  See changelog.d/README.md for the format and scoped exemptions." >&2
105	  exit 1
106	fi
107	
108	if [ -n "$shipped_files" ]; then
109	  shipped_count="$(printf '%s\n' "$shipped_files" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
110	  echo "✓ $added_fragment_count changelog fragment(s) added by this change cover $shipped_count changed shipped file(s)"
111	else
112	  echo "✓ no shipped surfaces changed; $fragment_count valid changelog fragment(s)"
113	fi

README.md
# Changelog fragments

Every pull request that changes a shipped surface must add a short Markdown fragment:

```text
changelog.d/<id>.<type>.md
```

- `<id>` is the Linear issue identifier in lowercase (for example, `mm-358`). If a
  change has no Linear issue, use the pull request number (for example, `271`).
- `<type>` is one of `added`, `changed`, `fixed`, `removed`, or `security`.
- The file contains one concise, user- or operator-facing Markdown statement. Do not
  include a heading or bullet marker; the release script supplies both.
- Use more than one fragment when a change belongs in more than one category.

Example (`changelog.d/mm-358.added.md`):

```markdown
Release notes now collect user-visible changes from pull requests automatically.
```

The CI gate requires a fragment when a pull request changes a deployable surface:

- server or shared runtime source under `crates/*/src/`, plus PDS runtime assets;
- either mobile app's frontend, native runtime source, static assets, or Tauri config;
- the public marketing site;
- the deployed MCP surfaces — the stdio Custos MCP server (`tools/mcp/src/`) and the
  credential-forwarding sidecar (`tools/mcp-sidecar/src/`, plus its image/config), which
  ships as a Railway service and re-exports the stdio server's tool surface;
- the notification relay's own image, entrypoint, and Railway config
  (`crates/notify-relay/`), which ships as a separate service;
- workspace runtime dependency manifests, the production image/config, or the NixOS
  runtime module.

Documentation, tests, design files, CI configuration, scripts, developer tooling, and
other repository-internal changes do not trigger the presence requirement. Any fragment
that is present is still checked for a valid name and non-empty content.

The browser test harness (`apps/*/src/lib/harness/`) is developer tooling despite its
path: it is double-gated on `import.meta.env.DEV && VITE_HARNESS` and proven absent from
production builds by `pnpm check:harness-absence`, so the gate skips it explicitly rather
than letting the broad `apps/*/src/` rule claim it.

`just set-version X.Y.Z` groups all fragments into a dated Keep a Changelog release
section in `CHANGELOG.md`, then deletes the consumed fragments. This README remains.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/skills/pr-review-comments

# Batch PR Review-Comment Triage

Pull every unresolved review thread on the current PR in one command, then triage the batch. The user should never have to paste review comments one at a time.

## Fetch unresolved threads

Determine the PR number for the current branch (`gh pr view --json number -q .number`), then:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){
  repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
    pullRequest(number:$pr){
      reviewThreads(first:100){
        nodes{
          isResolved isOutdated path line
          comments(first:30){nodes{author{login} body url}}
        }
      }
    }
  }
}' -F owner=<owner> -F repo=<repo> -F pr=<number> \
| jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[]
       | select(.isResolved==false)
       | {path, line, isOutdated,
          comments: [.comments.nodes[] | {author: .author.login, url, body}]}]'
```

Also fetch top-level (non-thread) review bodies and issue comments if the bot posts summaries there:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --json reviews,comments
```

## Triage the batch

For each unresolved thread, classify before fixing anything:

1. **Correctness / security / portability** — verify the claim against the actual code, then fix if real. Automated reviewers assert confidently and are sometimes wrong; refute with evidence when they are.
2. **Legitimate but out of scope** — file a follow-up issue rather than growing the PR.
3. **Pure style nit / preference** — decline with a one-line reason.

Present the full disposition table (thread → classification → action) to the user in ONE message before applying fixes, so they approve the batch rather than each item. Note that every fix-commit re-triggers CI and (for assertive bots like CodeRabbit) a fresh review round that tends to find one more micro-nit — batch fixes into a single commit where possible.

## Resolving threads

After pushing fixes, reply/resolve via:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='mutation($id:ID!){resolveReviewThread(input:{threadId:$id}){thread{isResolved}}}' -F id=<threadId>
```

(Include `id` in the reviewThreads query above if you plan to resolve threads programmatically.)

-- Durable tombstone for a parent's deletion of a sovereign child agent (MM-400).
--
-- Deleting a child reuses the deactivate + delete_after + reaper pipeline: the reaper eventually
-- calls account_delete::purge_account, which drops the child's account, repo, handle, blobs, the
-- agent_identities capability row AND (via the FK chain) the child's whole agent_audit_events
-- trail. So the child's own audit history cannot anchor "the deletion is auditable after the fact".
--
-- This table is that durable anchor (V030-style doctrine: the audit row survives the purge). It is
-- keyed by child_did but carries NO foreign key to accounts(did) on that column, so purging the
-- child's account row leaves it intact. It is anchored to parent_did (which DOES reference
-- accounts) so the parent's audit view outlives the child and the row is reclaimed only when the
-- parent itself is deleted (account_delete::purge_account deletes it WHERE parent_did = ?, never
-- WHERE child_did = ?). handle and registration_id are denormalized because their source rows are
-- purged with the child.
CREATE TABLE agent_child_deletions (
    child_did        TEXT NOT NULL,
    parent_did       TEXT NOT NULL,
    handle           TEXT NOT NULL,
    registration_id  TEXT NOT NULL,
    scheduled_at     TEXT NOT NULL,
    delete_after     TEXT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (child_did),
    FOREIGN KEY (parent_did) REFERENCES accounts (did)
);

| Finding | Disposition |
|---|---|
| "The short version:" opener in AGENTS.md | Fixed — the bot correctly cited our own new style guide |

23	A client reads `capabilities` and enables the matching features. Obsign, for

33	of these, and a well-behaved client falls back to standard AT Protocol behaviour.

64	device key is written into the DID's rotation keys from the very first operation.
65	This is the only way an identity is born already sovereign — the standard
66	`createAccount` lexicon never lets a client author its own genesis rotation keys.
67	
68	Without it, a wallet steers users to *import* an existing identity instead, and
69	the claim ceremony takes sovereign custody of an identity hosted anywhere.
70	
71	**Controlled by:** `signing_key_master_key`. The ceremony issues each account a
72	repo signing key and stores it encrypted under the master key, so a deployment
73	with no `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` cannot perform it and does not advertise
74	it. There is no separate switch: configure a master key (as any real deployment
75	should — see [Configuration](/operator/configuration/)) and the capability
76	appears.
77	
78	### `escrow`
79	
80	Custos holds one share of the account's 2-of-3 Shamir recovery split — encrypted,
81	and useless on its own — and releases it through the recovery gate: an emailed
82	one-time code, then a cancellable delay window during which the account holder is
83	notified and can abort. This is what makes recovery possible for a user who has
84	lost their device but still holds one share.
85	
86	Without it, the wallet's recovery story is entirely self-held: the user keeps
87	both remaining shares themselves, and no server is involved in recovery at all.
88	
89	**Controlled by:** `signing_key_master_key`. The stored share envelope is
90	encrypted under the master key, so a deployment without one cannot accept a
91	deposit or perform a release, and does not advertise the capability. The delay
92	window itself is tuned separately with `recovery.release_delay_secs`
93	(`EZPDS_RECOVERY_RELEASE_DELAY_SECS`, default 24 hours) — that changes how a
94	release behaves, not whether escrow is offered.
95	
96	### `sovereignSessions`
97	
98	Passwordless full-access sessions. Instead of a password, the client signs a
99	fresh, timestamped, nonce-bound proof with a key that is already in the
100	identity's current PLC rotation keys, and Custos verifies it against
101	plc.directory — never against a cached document. The account holder's device key
102	*is* the credential, so an account can have no password at all.
103	
104	Everything that needs a full-access session rides on this: app passwords,
105	changing a handle, removing an identity, restoring media from a backup.
106	
107	**Controlled by:** always. This is inherent to running Custos and has no operator
108	switch. It grants Custos no additional power over an identity — any current
109	rotation key qualifies, and rotation keys are the account holder's to control.
110	
111	### `agents`
112	
113	The [auth.md](https://github.com/workos/auth.md) agent surface: an AI agent or
114	automation registers with the server, the account holder confirms the claim from
115	their wallet (reading the exact scopes first), and the agent then exchanges its
116	assertion for narrowly-scoped, revocable, audited access tokens. Agent tokens can
117	never manage agents — including themselves — and every registration is revocable
118	from the wallet or by the identity provider.
119	
120	**Controlled by:** `agent_auth.service_auth_enabled`,
121	`agent_auth.anonymous_enabled`, `agent_auth.trusted_issuers`. These are the three
122	ways an agent can register, and **all three are off or empty by default** — an
123	untouched deployment does not offer agents at all. Enable whichever registration
124	flows you want (`EZPDS_AGENT_AUTH_SERVICE_AUTH_ENABLED`,
125	`EZPDS_AGENT_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED`, or a configured `[[agent_auth.trusted_issuers]]`
126	entry) and the capability appears. What a claimed agent may then do is bounded
127	separately by `agent_auth.granted_scopes`; narrowing it narrows every assertion
128	minted afterwards.
129	
130	### `walletConsent`
131	
132	An OAuth authorization can be approved in the identity wallet with a
133	device-key-signed decision, rather than by typing a password into a browser
134	consent page. The signed envelope binds the request, the client, the decision,
135	and the exact scope set, so an approval cannot be replayed onto a different
136	request, flipped from a denial, or widened after the fact.
137	
138	**Controlled by:** always. This is inherent to running Custos and has no operator
139	switch. Password-based browser consent continues to work for accounts that have a
140	password; the wallet path is an additional, stronger route to the same grant.
141	
142	### `optionalPassword`
143	
144	An account can be created on this server with no password at all. A client that
145	sees this capability may omit the password field entirely when creating an
146	account; the account is stored with no password hash and authenticates
147	afterwards through its device key — wallet-confirmed OAuth consent and sovereign
148	sessions — plus app passwords for standard AT Protocol clients like the Bluesky
149	app.
150	
151	Passwordless accounts are not a new storage shape: accounts that migrate in from
152	another server have always been stored without a password. What this capability
153	changes is only whether a *new* account may be created that way.
154	
155	An **empty** password is refused whether or not this is enabled, and that is
156	deliberate: an empty string is what an uninitialised form field sends, so
157	accepting one would let a client bug create an account with no credential that
158	nobody asked for. Omitting the field is the only way to ask.
159	
160	**Controlled by:** `accounts.password_optional`. Off by default — a passwordless
161	account depends on device-key custody you cannot verify on the account holder's
162	behalf, so a deployment whose users are not all running the identity wallet
163	should keep the password required. Enable it with `[accounts] password_optional =
164	true` (`EZPDS_ACCOUNTS_PASSWORD_OPTIONAL`) and the capability appears. Turning it
165	back off stops new passwordless accounts being created; it does not affect
166	accounts that already have no password, which keep working exactly as before.
167	
168	### `walletAccountDelete`
169	
170	An account can be permanently deleted with a device-key-signed proof from one of
171	its current rotation keys, in place of the account password. The emailed
172	single-use confirmation code is still required — this swaps one of the two
173	factors, it does not remove one.
174	
175	This capability is what makes `optionalPassword` safe to turn on. Deletion is the
176	one operation that had no route around the password: an account created without
177	one could be made, used, and migrated, but never removed, because every
178	credential path answered with the same refusal and left the holder no way
179	forward. The proof closes that.
180	
181	The signed envelope binds this server, the account, the signing key, the moment,
182	and a single-use nonce, and it is verified against the identity's **authoritative**
183	current rotation set read live from plc.directory — never a cached document. It is
184	accepted for accounts that *do* have a password too: a current rotation key can
185	already migrate or retire the identity outright, so it is the stronger credential,
186	and honouring only the weaker one would make the endpoint answer differently
187	depending on whether a password exists. Unknown accounts, wrong passwords, and bad
188	proofs remain one indistinguishable response.
189	
190	**Controlled by:** always. This is the same key-sovereign trust model as
191	`sovereignSessions` and has no operator switch; password-based deletion continues
192	to work unchanged for accounts that have a password.
193	
194	### `didWebHosting`
195	
196	Custos serves an opted-in account's `did:web` document at the account's own
197	domain (`/.well-known/did.json`) and emits an identity event so relays re-resolve
198	after an edit.
199	
200	Hosting is opt-in **per account**, never automatic, and only ever for a domain
201	the user controls: moving the document onto Custos trades away some of the
202	independence a self-hosted document gives an identity, so it is the account
203	holder's decision. Exit is a DNS repoint away.
204	
205	**Controlled by:** always. The server-side capability is inherent to running
206	Custos and has no operator switch; whether any given account uses it is that
207	account holder's choice.
208	
209	### `waitlist`
210	
211	A public interest-signup waitlist for a pre-launch deployment: an unauthenticated
212	`POST /waitlist` accepting an email address plus an optional atproto handle, meant
213	to be posted to directly from a marketing page on another origin (the endpoint is
214	CORS-open and carries no credentials). Signups are idempotent per email — a repeat
215	returns the same success and never discloses whether an address was already on the
216	list — and the handle is syntax-checked but deliberately never resolved, so the
217	endpoint has no outbound-request surface. The operator reads the list back with
218	`GET /v1/admin/waitlist` (newest first, with a total), which keeps working even
219	after the public endpoint is switched off again.
220	
221	**Controlled by:** `waitlist.enabled`. Off by default — an instance that isn't
222	running a launch funnel should not carry a public write endpoint it never asked
223	for. Enable it with `[waitlist] enabled = true` (`EZPDS_WAITLIST_ENABLED`) and the
224	capability appears; the per-IP signup rate cap is `rate_limit.waitlist_per_5min`
225	(`EZPDS_RATE_LIMIT_WAITLIST_PER_5MIN`, default 30).
226	
227	## Keeping this page honest
228	
229	The capability table in the server source
230	(`crates/pds/src/capabilities.rs`) is the single source of truth: it holds each
231	capability's wire name, the configuration that gates it, and the predicate the
232	server actually evaluates. The
233	[capability reference](/operator/reference/capabilities/) is generated from it,
234	and a CI gate (`just capability-docs-check`) fails the build if a capability is
235	added, renamed, or re-gated without this page being updated in the same change.
236	If a "Controlled by" line above disagrees with your server's behaviour, that is a
237	bug, not a documentation lag — please report it.
238

1 --- 2 title: Running a relay 3 description: Stand up the PDS, check its health, and understand what you are responsible for. 4 --- 5 6 The PDS is a single Rust binary with a SQLite database. It is designed to be 7 easy to host — the whole point of the project. 8 9 ## Health 10 11 Every deployment exposes a health endpoint the platform can watch: 12 13 ```sh 14 curl -sS https://your-pds.example.com/xrpc/_health 15 ``` 16 17 A healthy server reports its version, derived from the workspace version — the 18 same source these docs stamp — so the server and its documentation cannot claim 19 different versions. 20 21 :::note[Status is stated, not colored] 22 The operator console reports raw facts — version, uptime, counts, sweep 23 last-runs — and draws no `healthy`/`degraded`/`down` verdict of its own: the 24 thresholds are the operator's judgment, not the API's shape. What is wrong is 25 made legible in place — a troubled background sweep carries a trailing `!` glyph 26 and a named fault beside its figures, never a bare colored dot. A degraded 27 server tells you _what_ degraded. 28 ::: 29 30 34 35 On a degraded relay, the same readout flags each troubled background sweep with 36 a trailing `!` glyph and a named fault. A sweep whose last completed pass keeps 37 ageing reads `stale` — passes have stopped completing, so the sweep is dead. One 38 that completed but skipped work reads `failed ` — it ran, yet recorded `n` 39 errors (for blob GC, an account whose reconcile failed is skipped, so its blobs 40 stay uncollected until the fault is fixed). The two are named so they read apart on a 41 row that has both, and _what_ degraded is legible without relying on color. 42 43 47 48 ## Is the upstream relay seeing you? 49 50 A healthy server that no relay is crawling is invisible to the network — and an 51 upstream relay can silently drop your subscription. The console's Home screen 52 carries a **Relay federation** block that compares your server's exact sequencer 53 head against what the upstream relay reports for your host: the relay's 54 lifecycle status, its cursor, how many events it is behind, and when it last 55 consumed one. **Request crawl** re-invites the relay on demand — the recovery 56 move when the readout says the relay has stopped listening. 57 58 62 63 The same facts are served at `GET /v1/admin/relay-status` and the re-invite at 64 `POST /v1/admin/request-crawl` — see the [API reference](/operator/reference/api/). 65 66 ## What you are responsible for 67 68 - **Durability** — the SQLite database is the identity store. Back it up. 69 Production streams continuous backups to object storage with Litestream — see 70 [Backups & restore](/operator/backups/). 71 - **Availability** — users' clients reach your server to read and write. Health 72 checks and restart policy are your safety net. 73 - **You can't lock anyone in** — you hold the lowest-precedence rotation key; 74 the user's device key (`rotationKeys[0]`) and their recovery key outrank it, 75 so they can move their identity to another server whenever they choose. Design 76 your operations for that. 77 78 :::caution[Do not treat the DB as disposable] 79 Losing the database is not like losing a cache. It holds the repositories your 80 users depend on. Verify your restore path before you need it. 81 ::: 82 83 ## Deploy 84 85 The server deploys as an OCI image (Railway builds the `Dockerfile` directly). 86 The full runbook — staging vs production branches, Litestream backups, and the 87 security posture — lives in the repository's `docs/deploy.md`. 88

1 --- 2 title: Moderation 3 description: Takedown, restore, credential revocation, and account repair from the operator console. 4 --- 5 6 The operator console (the "Brass Console" companion app) exposes the moderation 7 actions an operator needs. Every action reports exactly what it did — the console 8 does not soften or hide the effect. 9 10 ## Actions 11 12 16 17 On the **Moderation** screen (look up an account by DID first): 18 19 - **Takedown** — stop serving an account: logins, writes, and sync are refused 20 until it is restored. 21 - **Restore** — reverse a takedown (the account resumes serving unless it is also 22 suspended or deactivated). 23 - **Credential revocation** — the incident-response follow-up for a compromised 24 account: in one sweep it revokes the account's **sessions, app passwords, OAuth 25 grants and pending authorization codes, and transfer-device tokens**, and reports 26 the literal per-family counts. The account's **main password is untouched**, and 27 any already-issued access tokens lapse on their own within minutes. Every holder 28 — including the owner — is signed out and must log in again. 29 30 You reach an account by tapping it in the account list, which is searchable by 31 handle or DID and shows each account's blob quota. 32 33 37 38 On the **Account detail** screen (reached by tapping an account in the list): 39 40 - **Correct an email** — fix an account's email address; this resets it to 41 unconfirmed. 42 - **Issue a password-reset token** — mint a single-use, one-hour reset token for 43 out-of-band delivery. This is **refused for a passwordless / key-sovereign 44 account** — those recover through their escrowed key share, not a reset. 45 46 Both takedown and credential revocation are destructive, so the console arms them 47 behind a two-tap confirmation that restates the target, then a biometric gate, 48 before anything is signed. 49 50 :::caution[Takedown is server-scoped, not identity-scoped] 51 A takedown affects what _your_ server serves. Because the user holds 52 `rotationKeys[0]`, they can migrate their identity elsewhere. Moderation is your 53 control over your infrastructure, not custody over their identity — keep that 54 distinction clear when you communicate an action. 55 ::: 56 57 ## Labeler watching — flagged accounts 58 59 Custos can watch ATProto **labelers** (moderation services) and flag any hosted 60 account they label. Flagged accounts float to the top of the console's account 61 list with an explicit `⚑` indicator per label — the label value, the labeler, 62 and when it was applied — and the Home screen shows a flagged-accounts notice 63 for the active server. This turns the account list from a neutral roster into a 64 spam/abuse triage view: if a labeler your network trusts flags one of your 65 accounts, you see it on your next glance at the console. 66 67 Watching is **off by default** — you choose which labelers' judgment reorders 68 your console. The recommended starting point is Bluesky's moderation service: 69 70 ```bash 71 # Environment form: comma-separated labeler DIDs, each watching every label value. 72 EZPDS_LABELER_WATCHED=did:plc:ar7c4by46qjdydhdevvrndac 73 ``` 74 75 or, in `pds.toml`, with an optional per-labeler watchlist (empty or omitted 76 `labels` means every label from that labeler counts): 77 78 ```toml 79 [labeler] 80 poll_interval_secs = 900 # default: 15 minutes 81 82 [[labeler.watched]] 83 did = "did:plc:ar7c4by46qjdydhdevvrndac" # Bluesky Moderation 84 labels = ["spam", "!hide", "!warn"] # omit to watch every label 85 86 [[labeler.watched]] 87 did = "did:web:some-other-labeler.example" # any labeler works, not just Bluesky's 88 ``` 89 90 How it works: a background pass polls each watched labeler's 91 `com.atproto.label.queryLabels` for your hosted accounts (the labeler's query 92 endpoint is resolved from its DID document), honoring label negations and 93 expiry, and reconciles the flagged state the console reads. The first pass runs 94 at startup, then every `poll_interval_secs`. The health readout reports the 95 watcher's last completed pass, so a stale pass is visible on the Status screen. 96 97 Two things worth knowing before you enable it: 98 99 - **Each poll discloses your hosted-account DIDs to the watched labeler** (they 100 arrive as the query's `uriPatterns`). Hosted DIDs are already publicly 101 enumerable via `com.atproto.sync.listRepos`, but watching a labeler does 102 establish a recurring outbound relationship with it — which is why this is an 103 explicit opt-in rather than a default. 104 - **A flag is the labeler's opinion, not a verdict.** Flagging changes only the 105 sort order and the indicator; it takes no action against the account. Takedown 106 and credential revocation remain your deliberate, gated decisions above. 107 108 Removing a labeler from the config (or disabling watching entirely) clears its 109 flags on the next pass or restart — flagged state never outlives the 110 configuration that produced it. 111 112 ## Accountability 113 114 Moderation actions are shown with their subject, the operator device that signed 115 them, and the result — status carried in text, not by color alone. Pair any 116 externally visible action with a clear, honest explanation to the affected user; 117 the tooling reports the literal truth, and so should you. 118 119 :::note[Per-device operator keys] 120 Operator actions are signed by a per-device key (Secure-Enclave-backed on real 121 devices). Revoking a device revokes its ability to act, per relay, without 122 disturbing the others. 123 ::: 124

2	title: Backups & restore
3	description: Continuous SQLite backups with Litestream, blob replication with the bucket mirror, integrity scrubbing, and how to restore.
4	---
5	
6	The PDS keeps its records in one SQLite database and its blobs (media files) on
7	the volume next to it, so backing those two things up **is** your
8	disaster-recovery plan. Custos uses [Litestream](https://litestream.io/) to
9	stream the database to object storage continuously and restore it on boot, and
10	its own **blob mirror** to do the same for blob files.
11	
12	## How it works
13	
14	When the Litestream environment variables are set, the container runs the PDS
15	under Litestream: it streams the SQLite write-ahead log to your bucket as writes
16	happen (not a nightly snapshot — a continuous replica), and on boot it restores
17	from that replica if the local database is missing. So a current restore point
18	always exists.
19	
20	The replica is defined in `litestream.yml` (committed in the repo) with
21	`force-path-style: false` — virtual-hosted-style addressing, which
22	Railway/Tigris-style buckets require.
23	
24	## Turning it on
25	
26	Set these on the environment you want backed up (production; staging and local
27	leave them unset and run the PDS directly):
28	
29	| Variable | Role |
30	| --- | --- |
31	| `LITESTREAM_S3_BUCKET` | The bucket the replica is written to. Setting this is what switches Litestream on. |
32	| `LITESTREAM_S3_ENDPOINT` | Object-storage endpoint (e.g. your Tigris/S3-compatible host). |
33	| `LITESTREAM_ACCESS_KEY_ID` | Access key for the bucket. |
34	| `LITESTREAM_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | Secret key for the bucket. |
35	
36	:::caution[The bucket credentials are secrets]
37	Store them in your platform's secret manager, never in the repository or the
38	image — the same discipline as the [master key](/operator/configuration/). Anyone
39	with the replica has a full copy of your accounts' data.
40	:::
41	
42	:::caution[The replica is only half the picture]
43	This backup protects the *ciphertext*. It does **not** protect the
44	[master key](/operator/configuration/) that decrypts it — back that up
45	separately, in a different store than this replica. If the key is ever lost
46	or compromised, follow the [master-key disaster runbook](/operator/master-key-runbook/)
47	instead of restoring from here alone.
48	:::
49	
50	## Blobs: the bucket mirror
51	
52	Litestream replicates only the SQLite database. Uploaded blobs — avatars,
53	post images, video — live as files on the deployment volume, where losing the
54	volume would destroy every account's media. The blob mirror is the Litestream
55	analogue for those files: a periodic sweep uploads every stored blob to an
56	S3-compatible bucket, and on boot the server attempts to restore any file
57	missing from the volume out of the bucket **before it takes traffic**. The
58	restore is best-effort per blob: a blob whose bytes exist in neither place, or
59	whose bucket copy fails content-hash verification, is logged loudly (per-CID
60	error plus a boot summary count) and boot continues — that blob stays
61	unavailable rather than blocking startup.
62	
63	Turn it on by setting a bucket (unset means disabled):
64	
65	| Variable | Role |
66	| --- | --- |
67	| `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_BUCKET` | Bucket the mirror writes to. Setting this is what switches the mirror on. |
68	| `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_ENDPOINT` | S3-compatible endpoint URL. |
69	| `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_ACCESS_KEY_ID` | Access key for the bucket. |
70	| `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | Secret key for the bucket. |
71	
72	The sweep also propagates deletions, on a lag: after blob garbage collection or
73	account deletion removes a blob's database row, a subsequent sweep deletes the
74	bucket object, so the mirror tracks the live blobstore rather than growing
75	forever (the worst case of the lag is the bucket briefly retaining collected
76	blobs). As a tripwire against acting on a wrong or empty database, a sweep that
77	finds no blob rows at all while the bucket has objects skips delete propagation
78	entirely. The full knob list (region, path-style addressing,
79	key prefix, sweep interval) is in the
80	[configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/).
81	
82	:::note[Same discipline as the database replica]
83	Blob bytes are content-addressed but they are still your users' data — keep the
84	mirror bucket's credentials in your secret manager, exactly like the Litestream
85	bucket's.
86	:::
87	
88	## Blob integrity: the scrub sweep
89	
90	A backup only helps if the bytes it protects are still good. A periodic **scrub
91	sweep** re-hashes every stored blob against its recorded CID and size, and walks
92	the blob directory for orphans in both directions — a database row whose file has
93	gone missing, and a file that no row owns. Bitrot, a truncated write, or a bad
94	restore surfaces as an operator alarm (the `blob_scrub_*` metrics and
95	`GET /v1/admin/health`) **months before a migration would trip over it**, rather
96	than as a mystery at the worst possible moment.
97	
98	When the [bucket mirror](#blobs-the-bucket-mirror) is configured, the sweep can
99	do more than report: a file that fails its hash or has gone missing is
100	**auto-healed** from the mirror's verified-good copy. Auto-heal is on by default
101	and has no effect when the mirror is disabled — with no verified copy to pull
102	from, a bad file is only ever flagged, never silently replaced. Both knobs
103	(`blob_scrub.interval_secs`, default 6 hours; `blob_scrub.auto_heal`) are in the
104	[configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/).
105	
106	Two guarantees close the loop around the sweep, so it catches genuine bitrot
107	rather than gaps the write and read paths should have handled themselves:
108	
109	- **Writes are crash-durable.** An uploaded blob is written to a temp file,
110	  fsynced, atomically renamed onto its content-addressed path, and the directory
111	  fsynced, *before* the database row is recorded. A crash or power loss can no
112	  longer leave truncated bytes at a valid path behind a row that already
113	  committed.
114	- **Reads are verified.** `getBlob` re-hashes a blob against its CID before
115	  serving it and returns a 404 (flagging the scrub alarm counter) on a mismatch,
116	  so a corrupted file is never handed to a downstream cache. A verified response
117	  carries the long-lived `immutable` cache header the blob spec recommends.
118	
119	## Restoring
120	
121	To restore the database from the replica:
122	
123	```sh
124	litestream restore <path-to-db>
125	```
126	
127	Litestream pulls the latest state (or a point in time) from the bucket. On a
128	fresh container the PDS does this automatically on boot when the local database is
129	absent.
130	
131	### Rollback after a bad release
132	
133	Schema migrations are **forward-only** — there is no down-path. Redeploying an
134	earlier `vX.Y.Z` tag is safe **only** when the schema change was
135	backward-compatible. If it wasn't, roll back by restoring the database from the
136	Litestream replica to a point *before* the promote, rather than by redeploying
137	old code against a newer schema.
138	
139	:::note[Inspect without rolling back]
140	To look inside the replica without touching production, restore a throwaway copy
141	and query it with `sqlite3` — no rollback required. The repository's operator
142	debug kit documents this runbook.
143	:::
144	
145	:::caution[Verify your restore path before you need it]
146	A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a plan. Do a restore into a
147	throwaway copy at least once so you know the bucket, credentials, and endpoint are
148	right before an incident forces the question.
149	:::
150

1 --- 2 title: Console screens 3 description: A visual tour of the Custos operator console — claim codes, accounts, devices, moderation, the audit log, transfers, and server status. 4 --- 5 6 A tour of the Custos operator console (the admin companion app). Every image here is 7 generated automatically from the app's own browser test harness across named scenarios, 8 including a degraded relay, so the pictures track the real UI and cannot quietly drift. 9 10 :::note[These are browser renders, not device captures] 11 These screenshots come from running the app frontend in a browser (the test harness), 12 not from an iPhone. Layout, copy, and states are faithful, but device-only details are 13 **not** pictured: the biometric (Face ID / Touch ID) gate that precedes every signing 14 action, the Secure Enclave-held admin key, camera QR scanning on the Pair screen, the 15 system share sheet, and iOS safe-area insets and font rendering. Treat these as accurate 16 diagrams, not pixel-exact device photos. 17 ::: 18 19 ## Home — mint a claim code 20 21 The console opens on the active relay, ready to mint a single-use, device-signed account 22 claim code. A **Relay federation** block up top reports whether the upstream relay is 23 actually crawling this server — status, exact events behind, last seen — with a 24 **Request crawl** re-invite (see 25 [Is the upstream relay seeing you?](/operator/running-a-relay/#is-the-upstream-relay-seeing-you)). 26 27 31 32 Before any relay is paired, the console asks you to pair this operator device. 33 34 38 39 ## Pairing 40 41 Pair a device with a relay by QR or manual entry. 42 43 47 48 ## Accounts 49 50 Every account on one relay, searchable by handle or DID, with a per-row blob-quota 51 readout. 52 53 57 58 ## Claim codes 59 60 The claim-code inventory splits live credentials from terminal history. 61 62 66 67 ## Devices 68 69 Every admin device registered on one relay — active and revoked — with a remote revoke 70 for a lost device. 71 72 76 77 ## Moderation 78 79 Account takedown and restore, then credential revocation — each an armed, biometric-gated 80 destructive action. 81 82 86 87 ## Audit log 88 89 Every privileged operator action — takedowns, credential sweeps, code mints and 90 revokes, device pairings and revocations, transfer cancels, account repairs, 91 crawl requests — is durably recorded with the credential that signed it: the 92 master token or the specific paired device. The Audit screen browses the trail 93 reverse-chronologically, filterable by action, with per-event drill-in by actor 94 or subject. 95 96 100 101 ## Transfers 102 103 In-flight device transfers an operator can watch and cancel. 104 105 109 110 ## Server status 111 112 One relay's health as it reports it — version and uptime, account counts, blob and block 113 totals, firehose state, and background-sweep last-runs. Facts only; nothing here is a 114 verdict. 115 116 120 121 On a degraded relay, a troubled background sweep is flagged with a trailing `!` glyph and a 122 named fault — `stale` when its passes have stopped completing (the sweep is dead), or 123 `failed ` when a pass ran but recorded `n` errors (for blob GC, an account whose 124 reconcile failed is skipped, so its blobs stay uncollected — and its disk unreclaimed — 125 until the fault is fixed). Naming each fault keeps the two 126 legible apart on a row that carries both; status is never signalled by colour alone. 127 128 132 133 ## Settings 134 135 Per-relay pairings, the global admin key, and the biometric toggle. 136 137 141 142 Further down, a **Diagnostics** section exports a redacted, per-relay network-error log for 143 troubleshooting — operation names, relay hosts, statuses, and short error codes only, never 144 credentials, keys, signed requests, or claim codes. 145 146 150

1	---
2	title: Configuration
3	description: The configuration and environment surface that tunes a deployment.
4	---
5	
6	A Custos deployment is configured through environment variables and a small set
7	of runtime settings. This page is the operator's map of that surface — the
8	knobs you'll actually set, with the context to set them safely. The exhaustive,
9	drift-proof inventory of every setting is the
10	[generated configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/), produced
11	directly from the server's configuration types.
12	
13	Some of these settings change what your server *advertises* to clients, not just
14	how it behaves: `describeServer` names the capabilities this deployment offers,
15	and clients enable features accordingly. See
16	[Capabilities](/operator/capabilities/) for which settings those are.
17	
18	## Secrets
19	
20	These are injected at runtime and never baked into the image:
21	
22	| Variable | Role |
23	| --- | --- |
24	| `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` | Master key (64 hex chars = 32 bytes) — the AES-256-GCM key that encrypts all at-rest signing material: every account's repo signing key, the server's OAuth signing key, the JWT secret, and the node identity. |
25	| `EZPDS_ADMIN_TOKEN` | Bearer token guarding the admin/operator endpoints. |
26	
27	:::danger[The master key must never change out from under the database]
28	The master key **is** the AES-256-GCM key those secrets are encrypted with; it is
29	used directly. Changing the environment variable alone on a populated instance
30	makes all existing secrets undecryptable — the server fails to load account repo
31	signing keys, and repo writes break. **Losing it is unrecoverable.** So: store it
32	in a secret manager (agenix / sops / your platform's secret store) never in the
33	repository or the image, and back it up.
34	
35	If it's already lost or you suspect it's compromised, stop and follow the
36	[master-key disaster runbook](/operator/master-key-runbook/) rather than
37	improvising — the recovery order matters.
38	:::
39	
40	Rotation is supported, but only as a deliberate offline operation: the
41	`pds rewrap-master-key` subcommand re-encrypts every stored secret from the old
42	key to the new one in a single atomic transaction, with the server stopped. Old
43	and new keys are supplied via `EZPDS_REWRAP_OLD_MASTER_KEY` /
44	`EZPDS_REWRAP_NEW_MASTER_KEY` environment variables (never CLI arguments), a
45	wrong old key aborts with no writes, and only after the re-wrap succeeds do you
46	point `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` at the new key and restart. Never rotate by
47	changing the environment variable alone.
48	
49	## Runtime
50	
51	| Variable | Role |
52	| --- | --- |
53	| `PORT` | Injected by the platform; the server binds it. |
54	| `EZPDS_PUBLIC_URL` | The externally reachable origin of the PDS. |
55	| `EZPDS_AVAILABLE_USER_DOMAINS` | Domains users may claim handles on. |
56	| `EZPDS_LABELER_WATCHED` | Comma-separated labeler DIDs to watch; hosted accounts they label are flagged on the operator console. Off (empty) by default — see [Moderation § Labeler watching](/operator/moderation/#labeler-watching--flagged-accounts). |
57	
58	The table above is the operator-facing subset. Every remaining setting — with
59	its type, default, and doc-comment — is in the
60	[generated configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/).

This surface reports the literal truth of what the machine is 8 doing — it does not hide the machinery. 9 10 If you are _using_ an identity rather than running a server, you want 11 [Using Obsign](/user/) instead. 12 13 17 18 ## What you run 19 20 - **[Running a relay](/operator/running-a-relay/)** — stand up the PDS, its 21 health, and what you are (and aren't) responsible for. 22 - **[Configuration](/operator/configuration/)** — the config and environment 23 surface that tunes a deployment. 24 - **[Moderation](/operator/moderation/)** — takedown, restore, credential 25 revocation, and account repair from the operator console. 26 - **[Master-key disaster runbook](/operator/master-key-runbook/)** — what to 27 do if the KEK is lost or compromised. 28 29 ## Which key you hold 30 31 The one thing to internalize before running Custos: you hold the **last** 32 rotation key, not the first. 33 34 ```text 35 rotationKeys[0] → the user's device key (highest precedence) 36 rotationKeys[1] → the user's recovery key (from their 2-of-3 backup) 37 rotationKeys[2] → the server's key (yours, lowest precedence) 38 ``` 39 40 Accounts created before on-device recovery keys carry two entries — the user's 41 device key, then yours — until their wallet adds the recovery key; your key is 42 last either way. The user can always override you. That is by design: it is what lets a user 43 leave your server without your permission, and it is the property that makes 44 hosting trustworthy rather than custodial. 45

MM-494 is done: [PR #497](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/497) is up, and Linear auto-flipped the issue to In Review with the PR attached (the branch-name convention did its job).

**What the pass did.** All eight hand-written operator pages got the PR #496 treatment — voice only, mechanism intact. Em-dashes went from 130 total to 37, and everything that remains is structural (the `- **Term** — definition` list idiom, table cells, one section heading). The prose tells I removed were the same three families as the user tier: self-defense asides ("that is by design", "and that is deliberate: …"), defensive adverbs ("exactly as before", "purely because"), and mid-sentence dash-appositives that read fine as parens or a colon. I also normalized the British spellings (`behaviour`, `honouring`, `uninitialised`, `colour`, `signalled`, `ageing`) that #496 already normalized on the user pages.

**The parity constraint turned out to be narrow.** `runbook-parity-check` locks three regex-extracted strings verbatim — the bolded golden-rule sentence and the two quick-reference ordering paragraphs — not the whole page. None of those needed voice fixes (the quick-reference arrow chains are exactly right for an incident checklist), so the site runbook could go 25 → 7 without touching the canonical engineering copy at all.

**Two scope notes.** One `behaviour` survives under `operator/reference/` — that's a generated page (`just docs-generate`), which the issue explicitly excludes; fixing it means touching the generator/source, a separate change. And I caught one self-inflicted hazard mid-pass: converting the screens.md frontmatter description's em-dash to a colon would have produced an unquoted YAML scalar with `: ` inside it, so it's reworded with a comma instead.

**Gates:** `runbook-parity-check` ✓, `docs-check` ✓, `ticket-ref-check` ✓, and `changelog-check` against origin/main confirms no shipped surface was touched, so no fragment needed this time.

I've had something in my mind while working towards opening this repo and project up to the public and inviting test users. I fear that the user-facing prose may come off too much as generated, and perhaps might not actually be targeting the correct audience. and then within the codebase, we often have dense comment blocks with a bunch of context that is vaguely useful-shaped but often just a lot to read. I can see how it may be useful for an agent, but I get this feeling that I have let it run away too far, and that we should take some corrective action. How might we approach these two problems?

This is exactly the kind of question worth grounding in real examples before prescribing anything. Let me load the relevant writing skill and then sample actual prose from the repo — docs site, marketing, in-app copy, and some of the dense comment blocks — so the assessment is concrete rather than vibes.
