Every image here is 7 generated automatically from the app's own browser test harness across named scenarios, 8 including a degraded relay, so the pictures track the real UI and cannot quietly drift. 9 10 :::note[These are browser renders, not device captures] 11 These screenshots come from running the app frontend in a browser (the test harness), 12 not from an iPhone. Layout, copy, and states are faithful, but device-only details are 13 **not** pictured: the biometric (Face ID / Touch ID) gate that precedes every signing 14 action, the Secure Enclave-held admin key, camera QR scanning on the Pair screen, the 15 system share sheet, and iOS safe-area insets and font rendering. Treat these as accurate 16 diagrams, not pixel-exact device photos. 17 ::: 18 19 ## Home — mint a claim code 20 21 The console opens on the active relay, ready to mint a single-use, device-signed account 22 claim code. A **Relay federation** block up top reports whether the upstream relay is 23 actually crawling this server — status, exact events behind, last seen — with a 24 **Request crawl** re-invite (see 25 [Is the upstream relay seeing you?](/operator/running-a-relay/#is-the-upstream-relay-seeing-you)). 26 27 31 32 Before any relay is paired, the console asks you to pair this operator device. 33 34 38 39 ## Pairing 40 41 Pair a device with a relay by QR or manual entry. 42 43 47 48 ## Accounts 49 50 Every account on one relay, searchable by handle or DID, with a per-row blob-quota 51 readout. 52 53 57 58 ## Claim codes 59 60 The claim-code inventory splits live credentials from terminal history. 61 62 66 67 ## Devices 68 69 Every admin device registered on one relay — active and revoked — with a remote revoke 70 for a lost device. 71 72 76 77 ## Moderation 78 79 Account takedown and restore, then credential revocation — each an armed, biometric-gated 80 destructive action. 81 82 86 87 ## Audit log 88 89 Every privileged operator action — takedowns, credential sweeps, code mints and 90 revokes, device pairings and revocations, transfer cancels, account repairs, 91 crawl requests — is durably recorded with the credential that signed it: the 92 master token or the specific paired device. The Audit screen browses the trail 93 reverse-chronologically, filterable by action, with per-event drill-in by actor 94 or subject. 95 96 100 101 ## Transfers 102 103 In-flight device transfers an operator can watch and cancel. 104 105 109 110 ## Server status 111 112 One relay's health as it reports it — version and uptime, account counts, blob and block 113 totals, firehose state, and background-sweep last-runs. Facts only; nothing here is a 114 verdict. 115 116 120 121 On a degraded relay, a troubled background sweep is flagged with a trailing `!` glyph and a 122 named fault — `stale` when its passes have stopped completing (the sweep is dead), or 123 `failed ` when a pass ran but recorded `n` errors (for blob GC, an account whose 124 reconcile failed is skipped, so its blobs stay uncollected — and its disk unreclaimed — 125 until the fault is fixed). Naming each fault keeps the two 126 legible apart on a row that carries both; status is never signalled by colour alone. 127 128 132 133 ## Settings 134 135 Per-relay pairings, the global admin key, and the biometric toggle. 136 137 141 142 Further down, a **Diagnostics** section exports a redacted, per-relay network-error log for 143 troubleshooting — operation names, relay hosts, statuses, and short error codes only, never 144 credentials, keys, signed requests, or claim codes. 145 146 150

1	---
2	title: Configuration
3	description: The configuration and environment surface that tunes a deployment.
4	---
5	
6	A Custos deployment is configured through environment variables and a small set
7	of runtime settings. This page is the operator's map of that surface — the
8	knobs you'll actually set, with the context to set them safely. The exhaustive,
9	drift-proof inventory of every setting is the
10	[generated configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/), produced
11	directly from the server's configuration types.
12	
13	Some of these settings change what your server *advertises* to clients, not just
14	how it behaves: `describeServer` names the capabilities this deployment offers,
15	and clients enable features accordingly. See
16	[Capabilities](/operator/capabilities/) for which settings those are.
17	
18	## Secrets
19	
20	These are injected at runtime and never baked into the image:
21	
22	| Variable | Role |
23	| --- | --- |
24	| `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` | Master key (64 hex chars = 32 bytes) — the AES-256-GCM key that encrypts all at-rest signing material: every account's repo signing key, the server's OAuth signing key, the JWT secret, and the node identity. |
25	| `EZPDS_ADMIN_TOKEN` | Bearer token guarding the admin/operator endpoints. |
26	
27	:::danger[The master key must never change out from under the database]
28	The master key **is** the AES-256-GCM key those secrets are encrypted with; it is
29	used directly. Changing the environment variable alone on a populated instance
30	makes all existing secrets undecryptable — the server fails to load account repo
31	signing keys, and repo writes break. **Losing it is unrecoverable.** So: store it
32	in a secret manager (agenix / sops / your platform's secret store) never in the
33	repository or the image, and back it up.
34	
35	If it's already lost or you suspect it's compromised, stop and follow the
36	[master-key disaster runbook](/operator/master-key-runbook/) rather than
37	improvising — the recovery order matters.
38	:::
39	
40	Rotation is supported, but only as a deliberate offline operation: the
41	`pds rewrap-master-key` subcommand re-encrypts every stored secret from the old
42	key to the new one in a single atomic transaction, with the server stopped. Old
43	and new keys are supplied via `EZPDS_REWRAP_OLD_MASTER_KEY` /
44	`EZPDS_REWRAP_NEW_MASTER_KEY` environment variables (never CLI arguments), a
45	wrong old key aborts with no writes, and only after the re-wrap succeeds do you
46	point `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` at the new key and restart. Never rotate by
47	changing the environment variable alone.
48	
49	## Runtime
50	
51	| Variable | Role |
52	| --- | --- |
53	| `PORT` | Injected by the platform; the server binds it. |
54	| `EZPDS_PUBLIC_URL` | The externally reachable origin of the PDS. |
55	| `EZPDS_AVAILABLE_USER_DOMAINS` | Domains users may claim handles on. |
56	| `EZPDS_LABELER_WATCHED` | Comma-separated labeler DIDs to watch; hosted accounts they label are flagged on the operator console. Off (empty) by default — see [Moderation § Labeler watching](/operator/moderation/#labeler-watching--flagged-accounts). |
57	
58	The table above is the operator-facing subset. Every remaining setting — with
59	its type, default, and doc-comment — is in the
60	[generated configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/).
61

1 --- 2 title: Running Custos 3 description: The operator's view — what Custos runs and how to run it. 4 --- 5 6 Custos is the server side: the PDS that hosts identities and the operator console 7 that manages it. This surface reports the literal truth of what the machine is 8 doing — it does not hide the machinery. 9 10 If you are _using_ an identity rather than running a server, you want 11 [Using Obsign](/user/) instead. 12 13 17 18 ## What you run 19 20 - **[Running a relay](/operator/running-a-relay/)** — stand up the PDS, its 21 health, and what you are (and aren't) responsible for. 22 - **[Configuration](/operator/configuration/)** — the config and environment 23 surface that tunes a deployment. 24 - **[Moderation](/operator/moderation/)** — takedown, restore, credential 25 revocation, and account repair from the operator console. 26 - **[Master-key disaster runbook](/operator/master-key-runbook/)** — what to 27 do if the KEK is lost or compromised. 28 29 ## Which key you hold 30 31 The one thing to internalize before running Custos: you hold the **last** 32 rotation key, not the first. 33 34 ```text 35 rotationKeys[0] → the user's device key (highest precedence) 36 rotationKeys[1] → the user's recovery key (from their 2-of-3 backup) 37 rotationKeys[2] → the server's key (yours, lowest precedence) 38 ``` 39 40 Accounts created before on-device recovery keys carry two entries — the user's 41 device key, then yours — until their wallet adds the recovery key; your key is 42 last either way. The user can always override you. That is by design: it is what lets a user 43 leave your server without your permission, and it is the property that makes 44 hosting trustworthy rather than custodial. 45

content.text:
This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The session's high-level purpose is **pre-public-launch corrective action on repo prose/documentation** for mal's ezpds repo. The durable spec is **docs/writing-style.md** (landed via merged PR #496); follow-ups were filed as MM-494 (done earlier in session → PR #497), MM-495, MM-496.

   The main request of this window: **"Work on Linear issue MM-495"** — full issue body provided: "AGENTS.md diet: map-not-territory register for the big files". Bring `crates/pds/AGENTS.md` (~15k words claimed, actually 16,624) and `apps/identity-wallet/AGENTS.md` (~10k claimed, actually 26,984) down to the register where an entry is a few lines — what the module is, the one or two facts an agent needs before opening it, and a pointer to the module doc. **Method (mal-approved via PR #496 pilot, ~3:1 compression):** (1) per file/section, first verify whether detail already exists in the module doc — where it does, pure dedup; (2) where AGENTS.md is the *only* home of a fact, **move it INTO the module doc first**, then shrink to a pointer — **never delete a fact that has no other home**; (3) per-file PRs; run `just ticket-ref-check` + `just docs-check` per PR. Expected 60–70% reduction with **zero information loss**.

   Follow-on requests: **"Coderabbit requested several changes on 499 in its review"** (handle the review batch) and **"a couple more nits from coderabbit, let's take a look"** (round 2).

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Map-not-territory register (writing-style.md): AGENTS.md = map; detail lives in exactly one home nearest the code (`//!` module docs in Rust, header comments in TS/Svelte); `crawler.rs`/`relay_status.rs` are the approved templates
   - Survey finding that inverted the issue's expectation: most pds files (all of auth/, identity/, lexicon/, most routes/ and db/) had NO module docs — the diet was mostly method step 2 (create docs), not dedup; the wallet files had rich `//` headers (Gathers/Processes convention) to MERGE into `//!` docs, never duplicate
   - Parallel agent fan-out (8 agents for pds, 5 for wallet, subagent_type "claude") with strict rules: `//!` after the `// pattern:` line + blank line, before any item (misplaced `//!` breaks compilation); preserve every fact (migration ids, config keys, error variants, invariants); no Linear ticket ids in .rs/AGENTS.md (ticket-ref-check gate); plain backticks; ≤~25-40 lines per doc
   - One serde wire-contract rule replacing ~25 repetitions: IPC error enums serialize as `{ code: "SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE" }` with camelCase fields; `$lib/ipc` TS unions must match exactly
   - Seven strict wallet pre-sign guards, each allowlist homed in its own module; sites without named guards (tombstone, recovery override, share-recovery rotations) document their *actual* constraints instead of inventing guards
   - changelog gate: `crates/*/src/` and wallet source are shipped surfaces even for comment-only diffs; fragment naming `<lowercase-linear-id>.<type>.md`; product name "Obsign" in wallet-facing fragments (CodeRabbit learning)
   - Worktree/devenv environment: no cargo in worktrees — main checkout devenv + `--manifest-path`; wallet host compile needs `EZPDS_IOS_BUILD=1` + `source apps/identity-wallet/scripts/ios-env.sh` + `SDKROOT=$(/usr/bin/xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-path)`; `NIXPKGS_ALLOW_INSECURE=1 nix develop --impure --accept-flake-config -c bash -c '...'`; real pnpm install in worktree via main devenv (never symlink node_modules); cargo fmt breaks in worktrees → `rustfmt --check --edition 2021` on explicit absolute file lists
   - gh/git network ops need `dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true`; Linear writes via the UUID MCP server `mcp__202234c8-...__save_issue` (plugin:linear:linear "unauthorized" is a decoy)
   - pr-review-comments skill batch flow: fetch all unresolved threads via GraphQL in one call, verify each claim against code, disposition table, single fix commit, resolve threads via `resolveReviewThread` mutation, reply on declines via `addPullRequestReviewThreadReply`

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - `crates/pds/AGENTS.md` — rewritten wholesale (16,624→5,260 words, −68%): Module Map one-liners, shrunk firehose/crawler/relay_status/rate_limit sections, identity/auth/db/routes tables with 1-2 line cells + "see module doc", metrics table collapsed to a paragraph pointing at `metrics::names`, Hard Rules + Adding-a-Route/DB-Query kept verbatim, "Last verified: 2026-08-02"
   - ~100 pds module docs created/extended by agents across `crates/pds/src/{routes,auth,db,identity,lexicon,read_after_write}/` and top-level modules
   - `crates/pds/src/firehose/mod.rs` — I added the "Emission map" paragraph (which routes emit which frames, genesis `#commit`+`#sync` staging, transitions-only `#account`, importRepo exception, pre-transaction `#sync` CAR build) before the "Module layout" paragraph
   - `crates/pds/src/metrics.rs` — module doc repointed away from the deleted AGENTS.md table + cardinality rule added; `pub mod names` doc changed to "the authoritative inventory of the instrument set"
   - `crates/pds/src/rate_limit.rs` — family-2 list brought current (native signup routes, waitlist, guess-target pairs sharing one limiter instance)
   - `crates/pds/src/routes/create_account_xrpc.rs` + `create_did.rs` — lock-ordering comments repointed at `firehose/mod.rs`'s module doc
   - `changelog.d/mm-495.changed.md` — "Server developer documentation moved from the crate overview into module docs beside the code it describes; no runtime behavior changed."
   - `apps/identity-wallet/AGENTS.md` — rewritten wholesale (26,984→3,818 words, −86%): harness section compressed to ~15 lines with pointers, one Rust module map table (~38 rows), frontend utility one-liners, single wire-contract rule, seven-guards pointer paragraph, cross-cutting Invariants only (bundle identity/access groups/iCloud container/constants), Key Files reduced to non-source entries, Troubleshooting kept trimmed
   - ~50 wallet files got module docs/headers from agents (all src-tauri/src/*.rs; keychain.rs = canonical Keychain account inventory; frontend headers in src/lib/*.ts, home-surface .svelte screens, +page.svelte step-graph HTML comment, harness scenarios.ts per-preset docs)
   - `changelog.d/mm-495-wallet.changed.md` — final content: "Obsign developer documentation moved from the app overview into module docs beside the code it describes; no runtime behavior changed."
   - **CodeRabbit round-1 fixes (commit b48626ca, 13 files)**: `identity_store.rs` (per-DID-methods-only registration precondition; remove_identity records `forgotten-dids` tombstone first, then index, then per-DID cleanup), `lib.rs` (ceremony staging "before the state-creating `POST /v1/dids` call — the read-only signing-key `GET` precedes it", both /// doc and inline comment), `share_ceremony.rs` (Share 2 escrow scoped to create/re-key; kit deposits nothing), `oauth.rs` ("`OAuthClient`'s DPoP mode has no production caller (Bearer construction still initializes the shared [`DPoPKeypair`], but Bearer requests never send DPoP proofs)"), `disaster_recovery.rs` (describeServer asked of the DESTINATION PDS; PLC state from plc.directory; dead source never contacted), `source_login.rs` + `password_unlock.rs` (password used only in `createSession` requests including the email-2FA retry with `authFactorToken`, never persisted), `password_unlock.rs` (unreached-probe rule scoped to the capability probe; `discover_pds` failure = plain NETWORK_ERROR), `recovery.rs` (no separate allowlist guard: counter-op derived entirely from pre-fork audit-log state, never caller input), `repo_backup.rs` (sig presence-checked, not verified against the DID key; destination importRepo authenticates), `identity_removal.rs` (tombstone constraints), `share_recovery.rs` (rotation ops copy verificationMethods/alsoKnownAs/services from authoritative state unchanged; only rotationKeys change via `anchored_rotation_keys`/`swapped_rotation_keys`), `+page.svelte` (flow map: `did_success → { did:plc: shamir_backup → handle_registration; did:web: handle_registration }`), changelog fragment "Obsign"
   - **CodeRabbit round-2 fixes (commit 1f269b9d, 2 files)**: `identity_removal.rs` — "so the pre-sign check is that self-verification alone; the separate lifecycle invariant is wiping local data only after the PLC submission succeeds."; `share_ceremony.rs` — staging boundary listed per ceremony: "the create ceremony's `POST /v1/dids` (the read-only signing-key fetch precedes staging), the re-key's rotation-op submit to plc.directory followed by the `PUT /v1/recovery/escrow-share` deposit, and the self-held kit's rotation-op submit (no `/v1/*` call at all — see `self_held_kit.rs` for its network posture)."
   - Memory files updated: `~/.claude/projects/.../memory/project_prose_style_corrective.md` (status: MM-494/495 in review, PRs #497-499; secrets-hook misfire gotcha recorded) + MEMORY.md index line

1	# Writing style guide
2	
3	Last verified: 2026-08-02
4	
5	Rules for every prose surface in this repo: the docs site, marketing copy, in-app
6	strings, code comments, and AGENTS.md files. The dream routine and doc-editing
7	agents follow this file; human PRs are reviewed against it.
8	
9	## Audiences
10	
11	**Obsign (user tier: `sites/docs` `user/`, in-app copy, marketing).**
12	Write for the *release* audience: security-minded people in the 1Password /
13	Proton lane, including people who are not technical but want better security
14	hygiene. The early test audience (peers, protocol-adjacent Bluesky users) can
15	read down to this register; the release audience cannot read up to a
16	protocol-native one. Concretely:
17	
18	- Lead with what can go wrong and how Obsign protects against it. Data
19	  ownership and sovereignty are outcomes the reader discovers, not the pitch —
20	  there is credible skepticism, even among protocol-minded users, that "owning
21	  your data" sells on its own.
22	- Protocol machinery (DID methods, rotation keys, PLC) appears only behind
23	  clearly-marked Advanced sections or on reference pages. A first-run page never
24	  requires it. The in-app register ("What's your situation?") is the model.
25	
26	**Custos (operator tier: `sites/docs` `operator/`, deploy/ops docs).**
27	A technical-minded subset of Obsign users who care how the technology works and
28	want full control over their data and presence. Keep the depth; these readers
29	want mechanism. The voice rules below still apply — technical is not the same
30	as dense.
31	
32	## Voice
33	
34	The failure mode to avoid is uniform, machine-flavored prose. The tells, and
35	their fixes:
36	
37	- **Em-dash budget.** A handful per page, not one per sentence. Most asides
38	  read fine as a separate sentence or set off with commas.
39	- **Retire the contrast scaffold.** "X is not Y — it's Z" and "not X, but Y"
40	  are fine once; as the default sentence shape they are a fingerprint. Say what
41	  a thing *is*.
42	- **No self-defense.** Cut asides that argue the design is right ("which is
43	  exactly the right time", "the trade is real"). Users need the task done, not
44	  the decision justified. Rationale belongs in ADRs.
45	- **Drop defensive adverbs.** "deliberately", "exactly", "precisely",
46	  "load-bearing" are for design docs. In user prose they signal an author
47	  anticipating an argument no reader is making.
48	- **Vary rhythm.** Short sentences exist. Use them.
49	- **Contractions are fine.** "It's" and "don't" read as human; "it is" and
50	  "do not" at every occurrence read as generated.
51	- Standard hygiene: active voice, concrete specifics over vague claims, no
52	  throat-clearing openers, no marketing adjectives ("robust", "seamless").
53	
54	The read-aloud test catches most violations: if a paragraph sounds like a
55	narrator defending a thesis, rewrite it as a person explaining a task.
56	
57	## Where prose lives
58	
59	One fact, one home. The repo's parity-check scripts exist because duplicated
60	prose drifts; the cheaper fix is not duplicating it.
61	
62	- **Code comments state constraints the code can't show** — invariants,
63	  ordering requirements, why an obvious alternative is wrong. They do not
64	  narrate what the next line does, and they do not argue rationale at length:
65	  link the ADR instead.
66	- **Don't restate what a test enforces.** If a test pins the behavior, the
67	  comment states the invariant in a line or two and names the test.
68	- **AGENTS.md is a map, not the territory.** An entry is a few lines: what the
69	  module is, the one or two facts an agent needs before opening it, and a
70	  pointer to the module doc. The detailed prose lives in exactly one place,
71	  nearest the code — usually the module doc. When consolidating, move detail
72	  *toward* the code and leave AGENTS.md pointing at it, never the reverse.
73	- **ADRs and design plans own rationale.** A comment or doc that finds itself
74	  explaining *why the design is right* should shrink to a link.
75	
76	## Enforcement
77	
78	By review, not by gate. Style is judgment work; the dream routine applies this
79	file on its nightly pass, and reviewers hold PRs to it. If a rule here proves
80	wrong in practice, change the rule — this file is the spec, not a monument.
81

1	# Marketing site — Obsign & Custos
2	
3	A static, zero-build marketing site: what Obsign and Custos are, what they do,
4	and the differentiators — cryptographic (not custodial) identity sovereignty,
5	tamper monitoring with the 72-hour recovery override, 2-of-3 Shamir backup, and
6	credible exit as a property of the keys.
7	
8	## Pages
9	
10	- `index.html` — the Obsign story, user-facing, with a Brass Console band
11	  introducing Custos.
12	- `custos/index.html` — the operator story: what Custos runs, how to run it,
13	  and the custody seam (`rotationKeys[0]` device / `rotationKeys[1]` recovery,
14	  both user-held / `rotationKeys[2]` server).
15	
16	## Social cards (Open Graph)
17	
18	Each page links a 1200×630 `og:image` (`summary_large_image`) so shared links
19	unfurl as a branded card. The images are generated, not hand-drawn: the HTML
20	sources (`assets/og/*.src.html`) use the same forked tokens and self-hosted
21	fonts as the pages — Obsign in the Sealed-Credential register, Custos in the
22	Brass Console. Regenerate with `assets/og/render.sh` (headless Chrome + the
23	pure-Node `pngcrop.mjs`; the script documents the 717→630 headless-crop trick).
24	`og:image` URLs are absolute against `obsign.org` (the apex).
25	
26	## Design derivation
27	
28	The two pages speak the repo's two scoped design registers — do **not**
29	cross-apply one to the other (see root `AGENTS.md` → Design Context):
30	
31	- The default register is **Obsign, "The Sealed Credential"** (root
32	  `PRODUCT.md` + `DESIGN.md`): archival white, sealing-wax gold + aubergine,
33	  Public Sans working voice, Libre Caslon Display as the once-per-screen
34	  signet, JetBrains Mono for every literal value.
35	- `.register-custos` scopes the **Brass Console** register (
36	  `apps/admin-companion/PRODUCT.md` + `DESIGN.md`): cool slate ground, lifted
37	  brass accent, monospace-forward prompt as the display voice.
38	
39	Tokens in `assets/css/site.css` are **forked from the live app token layers**
40	(`apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/styles/tokens.css` and
41	`apps/admin-companion/src/lib/styles/tokens.css`). Values must not drift from
42	those files; when a brief changes, re-fork.
43	
44	The Obsign register follows the system appearance: each color token is a
45	`light-dark()` pair forked from the wallet's dark appearance (§2 of root
46	`DESIGN.md`), and `:root` carries `color-scheme: light dark`. There is no toggle
47	and no JavaScript — the switch is `prefers-color-scheme` alone, so there is no
48	flash. The seal gold is appearance-invariant (the Same-Seal Rule) and every dark
49	text pairing is verified AAA, never eyeballed. The Brass Console (`.register-custos`)
50	is a **fixed dark register** — it does not follow the system in either place it
51	appears (the Custos page body and the Custos CTA band on the Obsign page).
52	
53	Web-scale extension: the app type scales are mobile-restrained, so the site
54	extends the same ~1.2 modular scale up two fixed-rem steps (`--text-display`
55	2.1rem, `--text-hero` 2.5rem), stepped down behind a media query — never fluid
56	`clamp()` (the briefs' fixed-rem doctrine).
57	
58	Held invariants: WCAG 2.2 AAA targets; status never color alone (color + icon
59	+ label + position); flat at rest (tonal layers + 1px hairlines, no resting
60	shadows); visible focus ring on every interactive element (aubergine on light,
61	gold on dark); matte gold, never metallic; `prefers-reduced-motion` honored;
62	fonts self-hosted in `assets/fonts/` (copied from
63	`apps/identity-wallet/static/fonts/`), no runtime CDN; no JavaScript beyond
64	the one self-hosted, cookieless analytics `<script>` (see "Analytics" below)
65	and the small inline waitlist-form handler on `index.html` (see "Waitlist"
66	below) — still no third-party scripts, ever.
67	
68	## Waitlist
69	
70	`index.html` carries the TestFlight interest form (`#waitlist`), posting
71	directly to the production Custos's public **`waitlist` capability**
72	(`POST https://pds.obsign.org/waitlist` — unauthenticated, CORS-open,
73	rate-limited; see the operator capabilities doc). Email required, atproto
74	handle optional; the handle is interest signal only (never resolved, never
75	touched as an account). The inline script is progressive enhancement — a
76	`<noscript>` note covers the no-JS case — and reports a single Umami custom
77	event on success (`waitlist-signup`, carrying only a `hasHandle` boolean; no
78	PII enters the analytics plane, per ADR-0029). The hero CTA click is tracked
79	as `waitlist-cta` via `data-umami-event`. The form goes live when the
80	production PDS sets `EZPDS_WAITLIST_ENABLED=true`; until then submissions get
81	the honest "isn't open right now" message (the endpoint 404s).
82	
83	## Analytics
84	
85	Self-hosted, cookieless, IP-anonymized page-view analytics (Umami — see
86	[ADR-0029](../../docs/architecture/decisions/0029-self-hosted-web-analytics-marketing-only.md)),
87	present on every page of this site only (`index.html`, `custos/index.html`,
88	`privacy.html`). It is a Railway service run alongside the PDS's other
89	services. `privacy.html` discloses what it collects and doesn't; the footer
90	on every page links it. Per the ADR, analytics never extends to the docs
91	site, either mobile app, the PDS backend, or any auth/PII surface.
92	
93	Umami's own website-level "Domain" setting is cosmetic only (it filters
94	self-referrals out of the referrer list; it does not gate the collection
95	API), so the embed carries `data-domains="obsign.org"` — Umami's
96	client-side hostname allowlist — to keep this site's non-production
97	deployments (Railway staging, local previews) from reporting into the
98	production dashboard.
99	
100	## Serving
101	
102	Any static file host — the site is plain HTML/CSS/fonts with no build step.
103	
104	Quick local preview:
105	
106	```sh
107	python3 -m http.server -d sites/marketing 8000
108	```
109	
110	Production is a Caddy container (`Dockerfile` + `Caddyfile`) deployed as its own
111	Railway service — a second service in the PDS's Railway project, scoped to this
112	directory (`Root Directory = sites/marketing`) so it stays independent of the
113	repo-root `railway.toml`. The `Caddyfile` handles gzip/zstd, clean URLs, and
114	cache/security headers. Full setup — including pointing the `obsign.org` apex at
115	it — is in [docs/deploy.md](../../docs/deploy.md) → "Marketing Site". To run the
116	container exactly as deployed:
117	
118	```sh
119	docker build -t obsign-marketing sites/marketing
120	docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 obsign-marketing   # http://localhost:8080
121	```

Hold the keys to your own identity.

89

90 Obsign is an iOS identity wallet for the AT Protocol, the network behind 91 Bluesky. The keys that control your account live in your device’s 92 Secure Enclave, not on someone else’s server, and your posts and media can be backed up to your own iCloud Drive. No platform, host, 93 or provider can take your identity, block your exit, or hold it hostage. 94

95
96 Join the TestFlight waitlist 97 Get the source 98
99

100 Open source, and in active development: iOS builds ship via TestFlight. 101

103

108

Owned, not rented.

109
110

111 On the AT Protocol, your account is a public record, controlled 112 by whoever holds its rotation keys. On most hosts today, 113 that’s the server. Your ability to leave, to recover from an attack, or 114 simply to stay yourself is a policy promise: real only for as long as your 115 host is honest, solvent, and online. 116

117

118 Obsign turns that promise into arithmetic. Your device holds the 119 highest-priority rotation key, so the final word on your account is signed 120 by you — and only ever by you. In addition, your wallet will create a recovery key, which is securely split into three shares, one stored in iCloud, one held in escrow by your server, and the third given to you to store offline. Only two-of-three shares are required to reconstruct the recovery key, so even if one share is compromised, the other two remain secure. A dishonest host cannot steal your recovery key, and you are able to fully recover your account from the two shares you hold. 121

How Obsign defends an account.

144

145 Set it up once, with care. After that, Obsign watches quietly, and if 146 something is wrong, it says so in plain words. 147

148

Sealed in your device

157

158 Your account key is generated inside the Secure Enclave and never 159 leaves it. It signs account operations only after you approve them: 160 reviewed on screen, confirmed with your biometrics. 161

It keeps watch

171

172 Obsign monitors the public PLC directory for changes to your account. 173 Every entry is verified against your own key: any operation you 174 didn’t authorize raises an alarm that tells you exactly what changed. 175

72 hours to take it back

185

186 Inside the directory’s recovery window, your device key outranks 187 every other key. One clear, reviewed action signs the override and 188 reclaims the account, before the window closes. 189

Backup without your server

200

201 At setup, your device creates a recovery secret and splits it into three 202 shares: iCloud Keychain, your server’s escrow, and a place you 203 choose. Any two bring your account back; no single share (and no single 204 company) can. 205

Leaving is allowed. That’s the point.

227
228

229 Because you hold the top rotation key, moving your account to a new host is 230 an operation you sign: it never requires your old server’s 231 permission, cooperation, or continued existence. Credible exit stops being a 232 promise in someone’s terms of service and becomes a property of the keys. 233

234

235 And nothing about this leaves the network behind: your server keeps a 236 lower-priority rotation key, so standard AT Protocol tooling and 237 ordinary migrations keep working exactly as they do everywhere else. 238

239

240 Turn on backup and leaving gets safer still: Obsign keeps your own copy of 241 your posts and media in your iCloud Drive — your records as a 242 portable snapshot, your photos and video byte for byte — so even a move 243 away from a server that has already lost some of your content isn’t a loss. 244

What if I lose my phone?

256

257 Your recovery secret is split 2-of-3 at setup: one share in iCloud 258 Keychain, one held in escrow by your server, one wherever you choose. 259 Losing the phone loses one share; any two remaining shares bring your 260 identity back on a new device. 261

Do I need to understand the cryptography?

265

266 No, and you’re never asked to. Obsign attempts to keep the process as simple as possible. If you want to understand what’s happening under the hood, Obsign gives you the details just a few taps away. 267

What about my posts and photos?

271

272 Your server backs up its records off-box continuously, and your media on a 273 regular sweep. And Obsign can keep your own copy of both — your posts 274 and your media — in your iCloud Drive, so your whole presence stays 275 with you even if the server that held it disappears. 276

Every pull request that changes a shipped surface must add a short Markdown fragment:

```text

Audit of `sites/marketing/` against [docs/writing-style.md](docs/writing-style.md) — the AI-voice tells and the framing rule (**security outcomes lead; data ownership is the discovered consequence, not the pitch**). ## Audit findings

**What already holds (untouched):**
- The Obsign page's IA is already security-led: problem → how it defends → credible exit → plain answers. The hero lede *ends* on the protection outcome ("No platform, host, or provider can take your identity…").

- **`custos/index.html` needed zero changes.** The Brass Console register holds: declarative, concrete, operator-tier depth where the style guide allows it. Its one contrast-scaffold ("Powerful enough to run your presence. Unable to take your identity.") is the once-per-page the guide permits, and it's on the OG card.
- No hype vocabulary anywhere ("robust", "seamless", "leverage", etc. — swept, zero hits). Em-dash budget within bounds on every page.

**What was adjusted (`index.html`):**
- **"Owned, not rented." → "Your account is a promise someone else keeps."** This heading was the one place ownership led as the pitch — exactly the framing the issue flags as not selling to the 1Password/Proton lane. The new heading leads with the risk the section actually describes; the body's payoff ("Obsign turns that promise into arithmetic… the final word on your account is signed by you") now *discovers* ownership. **What was corrected (`privacy.html`):**
- Factual fix: the page claimed analytics runs on "the two pages of this marketing site" while the script is on all three (including privacy.html itself). Now says so.
- "purely to distinguish" → "only to distinguish".

- Both changed pages rendered and read in the browser preview; text-only edits inside existing markup, no structural or OG-image changes.

Closes MM-496.

content.text:
MM-496 is complete: [PR #501](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/501) is open and the Linear issue is In Review with the PR attached.

**The audit's headline finding:** the site is in better shape than the issue feared. The Obsign page's structure is already security-led (problem → defense → exit → answers), and the Custos page needed **zero changes** — its Brass Console register holds cleanly. No hype vocabulary anywhere; em-dash budgets fine. The violations clustered in a few spots on `index.html` plus one factual error on the privacy page.

**What changed** ([index.html](sites/marketing/index.html), [privacy.html](sites/marketing/privacy.html)):

- **"Owned, not rented." → "Your account is a promise someone else keeps."** This heading was the one place ownership led as the pitch — the exact framing the issue says doesn't sell to the 1Password/Proton lane. The section body already tells a threat story ("real only for as long as your host is honest, solvent, and online"), so the new heading leads with that risk and ownership becomes the discovered payoff.
- **The recovery-key paragraph rewritten.** It was the most machine-flavored prose on the site ("In addition, your wallet will create a recovery key, which is securely split… Only two-of-three shares are required… you are able to fully recover"). Now plain active sentences with every fact intact: three shares and their homes, any two rebuild, the host's lone share is useless, your two bring the account back.
- Smaller fixes: the overloaded hero sentence split in three; the hedge "Obsign attempts to keep the process as simple as possible" removed from the cryptography answer; two defensive "exactly"s dropped; privacy page's "purely" → "only".
- **Factual correction:** privacy.html claimed analytics runs on "the two pages of this marketing site" while the script is on all three — including the privacy page itself. It now says so.

**What I deliberately left alone:** both hero h1s (custody framing, not the ownership pitch — and both are baked into the generated OG card images, so changing them would mean regenerating PNGs), the meta/og descriptions (they state a concrete security mechanism, not "own your data"), and the "It keeps watch" card's "exactly what changed" (that's an informative claim, not a defensive adverb).

Verified: `changelog-check` passes with the new `mm-496.changed.md` fragment, and both pages render correctly in the browser preview. That closes out all three writing-style follow-ups — MM-494, 495, and 496 are all in review awaiting your merge.

CodeRabbit requested some changes, and I'm also not convinced we moved far enough in the correct direction. With the user-facing docs, we trimmed quite a bit of the protocol talk in accordance with our audience statement, and those who are really interested in the protocol details are capable of reading down to the level as well as finding the more technical documentation. I'm not sure that the list of rotationKey indexes, for example, is really going to land with our launch audience

Two workstreams: the CodeRabbit round on #501, and a deeper de-protocol pass on the Obsign page (the style guide's own rule — machinery only behind Advanced/reference surfaces — applied with more courage). Fetching the review threads and checking how the keyfacts panel is styled, so I know what a de-jargoned version looks like:

Done — commit `4090a3f5` is pushed to [PR #501](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/501), and both CodeRabbit threads are replied to and resolved.

**CodeRabbit round: both accepted, both were real.**
- The share wording was factually off — [backup.md](sites/docs/src/content/docs/user/backup.md) says Share 1 lives in the **device Keychain**, with iCloud Keychain as the optional carrier. "One in your iCloud" overstated it, and the same drift pre-existed in two other spots on the page (the backup card said "iCloud Keychain", the phone-loss answer too). All three now say "your device's Keychain", and the phone-loss answer says "loses **at most** one share", which is both more accurate and more reassuring.
- The privacy contradiction was genuine: "nothing tracks you across visits" three lines before describing the same-day return-visit hash. Now scoped to "nothing follows you between sites or from one day to the next".

**The deeper pass — protocol vocabulary is off the Obsign page entirely.** A grep for `rotation|rotationKeys|PLC|2-of-3|did:` on [index.html](sites/marketing/index.html) now returns nothing:
- The keyfacts panel is no longer an array-index table. It's a plain who-holds-what: *your device* holds the deciding key sealed in the Secure Enclave, *your backup* is a recovery key split into three shares (any two rebuild it, no single custodian), *your server* signs posts and can never outrank you, and the *recovery window* is 72 hours. Same designed panel, same facts, no `rotationKeys[N]`.
- Body copy: "whoever holds its *rotation keys*" → "whoever holds its keys"; "highest-priority rotation key" → "the key that outranks all the others"; "the public PLC directory" → "the network's public record of your account"; "top rotation key" → "the deciding key"; "lower-priority rotation key" → "an ordinary key of its own"; "split 2-of-3" → "split three ways… any two".

The machinery didn't lose its home — the Custos page still carries the full `rotationKeys[0/1/2]` custody seam, one click away, which is exactly where the style guide says the protocol-minded reader goes to read down. "AT Protocol" and "Secure Enclave" stay on the Obsign page: one names the network, the other is a term the 1Password lane already knows.

Verified: changelog gate passes (fragment updated to describe the fuller change), rendered page reads clean in the preview. The push may draw one more CodeRabbit micro-round; I'll handle it the same way if so.

I've had something in my mind while working towards opening this repo and project up to the public and inviting test users. I fear that the user-facing prose may come off too much as generated, and perhaps might not actually be targeting the correct audience. and then within the codebase, we often have dense comment blocks with a bunch of context that is vaguely useful-shaped but often just a lot to read. I can see how it may be useful for an agent, but I get this feeling that I have let it run away too far, and that we should take some corrective action. How might we approach these two problems?

This is exactly the kind of question worth grounding in real examples before prescribing anything. Let me load the relevant writing skill and then sample actual prose from the repo — docs site, marketing, in-app copy, and some of the dense comment blocks — so the assessment is concrete rather than vibes.

# Writing for a Technical Audience

## Overview

**Core principle:** Technical writing must be clear, concise, and authentic. Clarity and technical depth are not opposites - you can have both. Avoid AI writing patterns that make content feel robotic or inauthentic.
￼
**Why this matters:** Developers value their time. Clear documentation builds trust. AI-like writing patterns (identified through research) make content feel generic and untrustworthy. Technical depth without clarity frustrates users. Clarity without depth leaves them stuck.

## When to Use

**Use this skill when:**
- Writing API documentation or references
- Creating guides, tutorials, or how-to content
- Documenting code, features, or architecture
- Writing technical blog posts or articles
- Reviewing technical content for clarity

**Trigger symptoms:**
- "Does this sound too robotic?"
- Writing feels formal or stiff
- Using phrases like "delve into" or "leverage"
- Explaining obvious things instead of getting to the point
- Uncertain if content is clear enough

## The Three Pillars

### 1. Clarity

Developers should understand on first read. No re-reading required.

**Techniques:**
- Short sentences (15-20 words average)
- Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences)
- Active voice over passive
- One concept per paragraph
- Define technical terms on first use

### 2. Conciseness

Every word serves a purpose. Remove noise and filler.

**Techniques:**
- Delete throat-clearing ("Let me explain," "It's important to note")
- Cut hedging language ("basically," "generally speaking")
- Remove marketing fluff ("powerful," "robust," "seamless")
- Use direct language ("use" not "leverage," "show" not "illuminate")

### 3. Consistency

Same terminology, structure, and voice throughout.

**Techniques:**
- Pick one term and stick to it (not "endpoint," "URL," "route" interchangeably)
- Use consistent code formatting
- Maintain same tone across all content
- Follow established patterns for similar content types

## Avoid AI Writing Patterns

Research shows specific phrases and structures that readers identify as AI-generated. Avoid these to maintain authenticity.

### AI Phrases to Never Use

| AI Phrase | Why It's Bad | Use Instead |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| "delve into" | Overly formal, 269x spike post-ChatGPT | "explore," "examine," "look at" |
| "leverage" | Corporate jargon | "use," "take advantage of" |
| "robust" / "seamless" | Vague marketing adjectives | Be specific about what you mean |
| "at its core" | Condescending simplification | "fundamentally" (use rarely) or delete |
| "cutting-edge" / "revolutionary" | Empty hype | Describe actual features |
| "streamline" / "optimize" | Vague promises | "speed up," "reduce," "improve" |
| "foster" / "cultivate" | Bland corporate speak | Use direct action verbs |
| "unlock the potential" | Cliched metaphor | State specific outcome |
| "in today's fast-paced world" | Generic filler | Delete entirely |
| "needless to say" | If needless, don't say it | Delete |

### Throat-Clearing to Delete

**Never start with:**
- "Let me explain..."
- "It's important to note that..."
- "It's worth noting..."
- "In essence..."
- "Let's explore..."

**Fix:** Start with substance. Delete the preamble.

### Hedging Language to Eliminate

| Hedged | Confident |
|--------|-----------|
| "I think we should..." | "We should..." |
| "It would be great if..." | "Please do X" |
| "Should be able to..." | "Can complete..." |
| "Basically..." | Delete it |
| "Generally speaking..." | Be specific or remove |
| "One might argue..." | "This indicates..." |

**Why hedging fails:** Makes you sound uncertain even when you're correct. State facts directly.

### Transition Word Overuse

AI defaults to formal Victorian-era connectors. Use simpler alternatives or break paragraphs.

| Overused AI | Better |
|------------|--------|
| Moreover / Furthermore | Plus, also, and |
| However / Nevertheless | But, though, still |
| Additionally | And, plus |
| Consequently / As a result | So, then |
| That being said | But (or delete) |
| Indeed / Interestingly | Often delete entirely |
| In conclusion | End cleanly without announcing it |

## Technical Writing Patterns

### Explain WHY for These Cases

**ALWAYS explain why when:**

1. **Design decisions with tradeoffs**
   - Good: "We use pagination instead of cursors because it's simpler for most use cases and maintains consistent ordering"
   - Bad: "We use pagination" (no context for when to deviate)

2. **Non-obvious patterns**
   - Good: "Row Level Security must be enabled on all tables exposed via the Data API because it enforces security at the database level, preventing bypass through direct SQL access"
   - Bad: "Enable RLS on all tables" (why?)

3. **Breaking from conventions**
   - Good: "This API uses POST for reads because GET requests can't include request bodies in some HTTP clients"
   - Bad: "Use POST to fetch data" (violates REST conventions without justification)

**When "how" alone suffices:**
- Mechanical steps with no alternatives ("Click Save")
- Standard practices ("Use npm install")
- When you genuinely don't know why (document behavior, note uncertainty)

### Code Examples: One Excellent Example

**Don't:**
- Implement in 5 languages
- Create fill-in-the-blank templates
- Write perfect-world examples with no error handling

**Do:**
- One complete, runnable example
- Include error handling
- Show realistic usage
- Comment WHY, not what

**Good Example Pattern:**

```python
# Good: Complete, realistic, explains why
try:
    response = await fetch_user(user_id)
    # Check status before assuming success - API returns 200 for "not found"
    if response.status != 200:
        raise APIError(f"Failed to fetch user: {response.status}")
    return response.json()
except NetworkError as e:
    # Network failures are retryable - log and re-raise for retry logic
    logger.warning(f"Network error fetching user {user_id}: {e}")
    raise
```

**Bad Example Pattern:**

```python
# Bad: Perfect world, no context, brittle
response = await fetch_user(user_id)
return response.json()
```

### Progressive Disclosure

Layer complexity. Simple first, then depth.

**Pattern:**
1. **Basic explanation** - what it does, core concept
2. **Simple example** - minimal working code
3. **Advanced section** - edge cases, configuration, tradeoffs
4. **Reference** - complete API surface

**Good:**
```markdown
## Authentication

All API requests require an API key in the Authorization header:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer REDACTED" https://api.example.com/users
```

### Advanced: Token Rotation

For production systems, rotate API keys every 90 days...
```

**Bad:**
```markdown
## Authentication

Authentication can be performed using several methods including API keys, OAuth 2.0, or JWT tokens. The choice depends on your security requirements, user experience goals, and architectural constraints. Let's explore each option...
```

(Too much upfront. Start simple.)

## Anti-Patterns from Real Documentation

### 1. Assumes Too Much

**Bad:**
> "Simply connect your ETLOrchestrator to the HydraNode endpoint. Once a connection is established, instantiate a DataStream by passing your KinesisConfiguration."

**Why it fails:** Jargon firehose with no definitions, no links, no onramp for beginners.

**Fix:** Define terms, link to prerequisites, provide Getting Started guide.

### 2. Perfect World Examples

**Bad:**
```javascript
const myFile = document.getElementById('file-input').files[0];
const response = await uploadFile('/api/upload', myFile);
console.log('File uploaded successfully!');
```

**Why it fails:** No error handling, ignores edge cases (no file selected, network failure, file too large).

**Fix:** Wrap in try-catch, check response status, handle undefined files.

### 3. Vague and Unhelpful

**Bad:**
- `getUser(userId)`: "Gets a user by their ID."
- `class DataProcessor`: "A class for processing data."
- `processData(data)`: "Processes the data."

**Why it fails:** Tautological. Says nothing beyond the function name.

**Fix:** Describe behavior, parameters, return values, exceptions. "Fetches user record from database, returns null if user doesn't exist. Throws AuthError if API key lacks read permissions."

## Pro-Examples from Industry Leaders

### Supabase (Clarity + Depth)

> "Row Level Security (RLS) is a PostgreSQL feature that allows you to control which rows a user can access in a table. When you enable RLS on a table, all SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations are subject to a security policy. A policy is a SQL expression that returns a boolean value. If the expression returns true, the operation is allowed to proceed. If it returns false or null, the operation is denied."

**Why it works:** Defines RLS, explains scope (CRUD operations), defines mechanism (policy = SQL boolean expression). Dense with information, perfectly clear.

### Stripe (Predictable Contract)

> "Stripe uses conventional HTTP response codes to indicate the success or failure of an API request. In general: Codes in the 2xx range indicate success. Codes in the 4xx range indicate an error that failed given the information provided. Codes in the 5xx range indicate an error with Stripe's servers."

**Why it works:** Establishes predictable contract for fundamental API behavior. Technical, precise, immediately useful.

### Astro (Anticipates Questions)

> "You can run create-astro anywhere on your machine, so you don't have to create an empty directory for your project first. If you don't have an empty directory yet, the wizard will help you create one."

**Why it works:** Anticipates common beginner question ("Do I need to make a folder first?") and answers it proactively.

### Tailwind CSS (Teaches Philosophy)

> "The biggest maintainability concern when using a utility-first approach is managing commonly repeated utility combinations. The traditional approach is to extract repeated utilities into a component class. We believe that @apply should be used sparingly. The best way to manage repeated utility combinations is to create reusable components with a templating language."

**Why it works:** Identifies problem, presents common solution, explains why that solution is suboptimal, guides toward better approach. Teaches philosophy, not just features.

## Writing That Feels Human

### Use Contractions

**AI defaults to:**
- "It is important that you do not..."
- "You will need to..."

**Human writing:**
- "It's important that you don't..."
- "You'll need to..."

### Vary Sentence Length

**AI writes:**
Every paragraph is 3-4 sentences. Every sentence is 15-20 words. Everything feels perfectly balanced and rhythmic in an uncanny way.

**Human writes:**
Short sentences create emphasis. Longer sentences provide context, explanation, or explore nuance that requires more breathing room. Mix them. Create rhythm naturally.

### Add Personality

**AI avoids:**
- First person ("I," "we")
- Opinions
- Personal anecdotes
- Humor

**Human includes:**
- "We tried the obvious solution first and it failed"
- "I found this approach more practical because..."
- Opinions grounded in experience
- Self-aware observations

### Break Grammar Rules Intentionally

**AI never:**
- Starts sentences with "And" or "But"
- Uses sentence fragments
- Ends with prepositions

**Human does:**
- "And that's exactly the point." (emphasis)
- "This is what we're dealing with." (natural)

### Be Specific

**AI writes vaguely:**
- "This approach offers significant benefits"
- "Companies have seen improved results"

**Human writes specifically:**
- "We reduced latency from 450ms to 120ms"
- "Three team members raised concerns about X"

## Code Comments and Documentation

### Punctuation

Always use periods at the end of code comments.

```typescript
// Good: Validates user input before processing.
// Bad: validates user input before processing
```

### Headings

Use sentence case in all headings. Never title case.

```markdown
Good: ## Error handling patterns
Bad:  ## Error Handling Patterns

Good: ### When to use async
Bad:  ### When To Use Async
```

### Error Messages

Format error messages as lowercase sentence fragments. They compose naturally when chained.

```
Good: failed to parse configuration: invalid JSON at line 42
Bad:  Failed to Parse Configuration: Invalid JSON at Line 42
```

The lowercase format works because errors often chain: `"operation failed: " + innerError.message` reads correctly.

## Red Flags - Review Checklist

Before publishing, check for these issues:

- [ ] No AI phrases ("delve," "leverage," "robust," "at its core")
- [ ] No throat-clearing openings ("Let me explain," "It's important to note")
- [ ] No hedging language ("basically," "generally speaking")
- [ ] No marketing fluff ("powerful," "revolutionary," "cutting-edge")
- [ ] Sentence length varies (not all 15-20 words)
- [ ] Paragraph length varies (not all 3-4 sentences)
- [ ] Contractions used naturally ("it's" not "it is")
- [ ] Active voice, clear actors (not "it can be seen that")
- [ ] Code examples include error handling
- [ ] WHY explained for design decisions
- [ ] Technical terms defined on first use
- [ ] Specific numbers/names/details (not vague claims)
- [ ] Read aloud test - does it sound natural?
- [ ] Code comments end with periods
- [ ] Headings use sentence case (not Title Case)
- [ ] Error messages are lowercase sentence fragments

## Common Mistakes and Fixes

| Mistake | Reality | Fix |
|---------|---------|-----|
| "Just being thorough with explanations" | You're explaining obvious things. | Delete explanations of what developers already know. |
| "Keeping it professional with formal language" | Formal = robotic. | Use contractions, conversational tone, natural language. |
| "Covering all the edge cases upfront" | Overwhelms reader. | Basic case first, advanced section for edge cases. |
| "Using precise technical terminology" | Jargon without definitions loses readers. | Define terms on first use, link to glossary. |
| "Being careful with hedging language" | Hedging makes you sound uncertain. | State facts directly. Remove qualifiers. |
| "Perfect code examples look cleaner" | Perfect world examples are brittle in practice. | Include error handling, show realistic usage. |
| "More examples = more helpful" | Too many examples = noise. | One excellent, complete example beats five shallow ones. |

## Summary

**Technical writing in three rules:**

1. **Clear and concise** - Short sentences, short paragraphs, active voice, no filler
2. **Authentic voice** - Contractions, varied rhythm, personality, specific details
3. **Explain why** - Design decisions, tradeoffs, non-obvious patterns need justification

**Avoid AI markers:** No "delve," "leverage," "robust." No throat-clearing. No hedging. No formal transitions.

**One excellent example** beats five mediocre ones. Include error handling. Show realistic usage.

**Technical depth + clarity are not opposites.** You can have both. Supabase, Stripe, and Cloudflare prove this daily.

**Read aloud test:** If it sounds robotic or overly formal, rewrite it.

Your device becomes its master key; the account stays on 18 its current server. 19 - **I lost access to my wallet** — bring an identity back onto a new device using 20 any two of its three backup shares (see 21 [Recovering with two shares](/user/backup/#recovering-with-two-shares)). 22 - **My server is gone** — your host has disappeared and you need the identity 23 somewhere else. 24 25 Taking custody of an existing account is not the same as moving it. It changes 26 *who holds the keys*; moving changes *where the account lives*, and you do that 27 later from the identity's own screen (see 28 [Migrating your identity](/user/migration/)). 29 30 If you already have identities in the wallet, tap **Add an identity** at the 31 bottom of your identity list to reach this screen again. 32 33 37 38 ## Create an identity 39 40 1. Open Obsign and choose **Starting fresh**. 41 2. Follow the prompts to pick a handle on an available domain and set up your 42 account. 43 3. Obsign generates your identity key **on your device** and seals it. The key 44 never leaves your device unencrypted. 45 4. As part of setup, Obsign walks you through **backing up your recovery key** and 46 won't let you finish until you've saved your share — see 47 [2-of-3 Shamir backup](/user/backup/). 48 49 :::tip 50 Backup isn't a separate step you do later — it's built into adding your identity, 51 which is exactly the right time. Save your share somewhere durable when Obsign 52 prompts you, not after you've lost a device. 53 ::: 54 55 :::note 56 Creating an identity needs a **Custos** server. Your device has to author the 57 identity's very first record and hold its master key from that moment on, and a 58 standard ATProtocol server has no way to accept that — it can only create 59 accounts where the server holds the key. If you point Obsign at another server, 60 it says so on the server screen, before you fill anything in, and offers to 61 import an identity there instead. 62 ::: 63 64 ## Import an identity 65 66 If you already have an ATProtocol identity — on [bsky.social](https://bsky.social), 67 a self-hosted PDS, anywhere — choose **I have an account somewhere**. Obsign installs this 68 device's key as the identity's master key, which is what unlocks tamper 69 monitoring, the 72-hour reversal window, and your own backups. The account itself 70 does not move: it keeps running on the same server, with the same handle. 71 72 Importing works against any spec-compliant server, Custos or not. 73 74 Moving the account to a different server is a separate decision you can make 75 later, from the identity's own screen: [Migrating your 76 identity](/user/migration/). 77 78 ## Advanced: anchor to a domain you control (did:web) 79 80 By default, a new identity is a **did:plc** — an entry in ATProtocol's public 81 PLC directory. That is the right choice for almost everyone, and everything 82 else in these docs assumes it. 83 84 If you already run a domain, Obsign also offers **did:web**: your identity 85 becomes `did:web:your-domain.example`, anchored to a DID document served from 86 that domain rather than to the PLC directory. The wallet walks you through 87 composing the document, proves you control the domain by requiring the exact 88 reviewed document to be live at its authoritative HTTPS URL before the server 89 accepts it, and can either let your server host the document for you or leave 90 you hosting it yourself. 91 92 The trade is real, which is why it sits behind an "Advanced" link: 93 94 - **You gain** an identity rooted in something you already own. No directory, 95 and no server, sits between you and it. 96 - **You take on** the domain as part of your security perimeter. A did:web 97 identity has no PLC rotation keys, so the 98 [tamper monitoring and 72-hour override](/user/recovery/) and the 99 [2-of-3 share backup](/user/backup/) do not apply — recovery is controlling 100 the domain (plus your device key), and losing the domain means losing the 101 identity. 102 103 ## The custody model, briefly 104 105 Your identity is anchored by rotation keys, in order of precedence: 106 107 - `rotationKeys[0]` — **yours**, held by Obsign on your device. 108 - `rotationKeys[1]` — your **recovery key**, derived from the secret your 109 [2-of-3 Shamir backup](/user/backup/) protects. Your device creates it; the 110 server never sees it. 111 - `rotationKeys[2]` — the server's, used only for routine operations. 112 113 You can see them on an identity's DID document screen — `#rotation-0` is your 114 device key, and the server's key always sits last. 115 116 120 121 Because your key outranks the server's, you can always override the server. That 122 ordering is what makes _credible exit_ a property of the keys, not a promise. 123

2	//
3	//! `repo_seq` firehose event-log retention.
4	//!
5	//! A periodic background task that prunes the durable firehose event log (`repo_seq`, added by
6	//! V028) so it does not grow without bound. Every `#commit` and `#account` frame — including each
7	//! commit's CARv1 `blocks` — is retained in `repo_seq` so `com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos` cursor
8	//! replay survives restarts (see `firehose.rs`). Without a sweep the table is append-only and
9	//! would eventually dominate the production SQLite DB and the Litestream backup.
10	//!
11	//! ## Policy (union — the most aggressive enabled retention bounds growth)
12	//!
13	//! On each pass the sweep computes a **low-water mark** below which rows are prunable, from the
14	//! enabled retention knobs (see [`FirehoseConfig`](common::FirehoseConfig)):
15	//!
16	//! * **Age** (`log_retention_secs`): rows whose `sequenced_at` is older than `now − retention`
17	//!   are prunable. The age watermark is `first_retained_seq − 1`, where `first_retained_seq` is
18	//!   `MIN(seq)` among rows *at or after* the cutoff (see [`firehose_seq::retained_boundary_seq`]);
19	//!   if no row is retained by age, the whole log is prunable up to the frontier.
20	//! * **Count** (`log_retention_count`): keep at most the newest `N` rows, i.e. the watermark is
21	//!   `MAX(seq) − N`.
22	//!
23	//! The combined watermark is the **`max`** of the enabled policies' contributions: a row is
24	//! pruned when it falls below **any** enabled cutoff, so enabling both knobs bounds growth by
25	//! whichever policy fires (age prunes old rows even when count would keep them; count prunes a
26	//! huge young backlog even when age would keep it). A `0` knob disables that policy and
27	//! contributes nothing; both at `0` makes the sweep a no-op (the log stays append-only, exactly
28	//! the pre-retention behaviour).
29	//!
30	//! The age boundary is deliberately computed from the first *retained* seq rather than
31	//! `MAX(seq)` among old rows, so a row with a skewed-old timestamp can never lift the watermark
32	//! past fresh rows (an over-prune / data loss). The worst case under non-monotonic timestamps is
33	//! that an oddly-timestamped row lingers — an under-prune the next pass corrects.
34	//!
35	//! ## Invariants preserved
36	//!
37	//! * **The live frontier is never pruned.** The watermark is clamped to `MAX(seq) − 1`, so a
38	//!   reconnecting relay can always resume from at least the newest retained event and `read_replay`
39	//!   can always reach the frontier it snapshotted.
40	//! * **`seq` stays monotonic and is never reused.** `seq` is the explicit `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`,
41	//!   so a pruned number is gone for good; the sequencer keeps advancing from its in-memory

content.text:
Done sampling. I looked at the user docs (all 8 pages plus operator pages), the marketing/in-app copy, the biggest comment blocks in `crates/pds`, and — helpfully — the two AGENTS.md files that auto-loaded into my own context while I worked, which turned out to be the best evidence for problem two. Here's my read.

## Problem 1: the user-facing prose

Your instinct is right, but the diagnosis is more specific than "sounds generated." The writing is actually *good* in ways that matter — concrete, honest, explains real trade-offs. What makes it read as generated is that every page has the **same voice**, and that voice has measurable tells. From [getting-started.md](sites/docs/src/content/docs/user/getting-started.md) alone:

- **Em-dash density**: 19–29 per ~1,000 words on most user pages. Human technical writing runs maybe 2–5.
- **The contrast construction**, over and over: "Taking custody of an existing account is not the same as moving it. It changes *who holds the keys*; moving changes *where the account lives*." Once per page is style; three times per page is a fingerprint.
- **Self-justifying asides**: "which is exactly the right time," "The trade is real, which is why it sits behind an 'Advanced' link." The docs constantly *defend the design* to the reader. Users don't need the design defended — they need the task done. This voice leaked in from the ADR-writing process, where arguing rationale is the whole point.

The deeper issue is the **audience question** you raised. The getting-started page — the first thing a test user reads — reaches `rotationKeys[0]`, DID documents, and a did:web trade-off analysis by screen two. Meanwhile the in-app copy ([AddIdentityScreen.svelte](apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/components/onboarding/AddIdentityScreen.svelte)) is genuinely excellent: "What's your situation?" / "Starting fresh" / "I lost access to my wallet." The app talks to a person; the docs talk to a protocol-curious peer. Per your own DESIGN.md, Obsign is in the Proton/1Password lane — and 1Password's user docs never show you a key index.

**Approach I'd recommend:**

1. **You write the audience statement first** — this is the one input only you can provide, and everything else keys off it. Two or three sentences per docs tier: who is the `user/` reader (a Bluesky user who saw "own your identity" and clicked, or an early-adopter who already knows what a PDS is?), and who is the `operator/` reader. My guess is your *actual* first test users are protocol-adjacent, which might mean the current depth is right and only the voice needs fixing — but that's your call, not mine.
2. **Distill a one-page style guide** from the tells above (em-dash budget, ban the contrast construction as a crutch, cut self-justifying asides, protocol vocabulary only behind "Advanced" sections in user docs). I'd anchor it on the `writing-for-a-technical-audience` house-style skill that's already installed — it covers most of this.
3. **Rewrite page-by-page with you reviewing**, user tier first (it's only ~6,000 words total — this is a day of work, not a project). The read-aloud test catches most of it.
4. **Fix the source, not just the output**: the nightly dream routine PRs documentation edits, and it writes in exactly this voice. If its instructions don't get the style guide, the voice regrows one merged PR at a time.

## Problem 2: the comment blocks

Here I'd split what you're feeling into three different things, because the right action differs:

**In-code module docs** — e.g. [firehose_gc.rs](crates/pds/src/firehose_gc.rs) opens with 49 lines of policy and invariants. Content-wise this is mostly *legitimate*: invariants like "the live frontier is never pruned" are exactly what a module doc is for on GC code. The bloat is the narrative rationale woven in ("deliberately computed from… so a skewed-old timestamp can never…"). That's ADR material, and you have an ADR log. Rule of thumb: **comments state constraints; ADRs argue decisions; the comment links to the ADR.**

**Comments that duplicate enforcement** — [account_delete.rs:38](crates/pds/src/account_delete.rs) carries 47 lines documenting FK deletion order… and then names the schema-walking test that *enforces* that order. The test is the durable artifact; half that comment is a prose shadow of it and will drift. These can be cut hard: state the invariant in two lines, point at the test.

**AGENTS.md files — this is the actual runaway.** [crates/pds/AGENTS.md](crates/pds/AGENTS.md) is ~15,000 words; [apps/identity-wallet/AGENTS.md](apps/identity-wallet/AGENTS.md) ~10,000. Both loaded into my context this session and consumed a large fraction of it. The route table has paragraph-long cells that restate what the route file (and its own comments!) already say — three copies of every fact, and the repo's growing collection of parity-check scripts is the immune response to the drift that duplication guarantees. The fix isn't deletion, it's **demotion to pointers**: one line per route ("`oauth_consent.rs` — wallet-confirmed OAuth consent; envelope + match-code details in the file's module doc"), with prose living in exactly one home, nearest the code. I'd expect a 60–70% reduction with zero information loss, and an *improvement* for agents — a map you can hold in your head beats a territory-sized map.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
There's a self-reinforcing loop worth naming: agents wrote dense docs → dense docs load into every future agent's context → those agents learn "this repo's register is exhaustive" → they write denser docs. The dream routine and AGENTS.md conventions are the loop's feedback path, which is why updating *instructions* (style guide, comment rules) matters more than any one-time cleanup — a cleanup without the instruction change just resets the clock.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Suggested sequence

1. You draft the audience statement (the one blocking input).
2. I distill the style guide + comment rules into a short section of AGENTS.md and the dream routine's instructions.
3. Pilot before sweeping: I rewrite **one** user doc page and diet **one** AGENTS.md section, you review the before/after, we calibrate, then sweep the rest.
4. Capture the sweep as Linear issues per your capture-before-close convention.

Want me to start with the pilot pair so you have something concrete to react to, or would you rather nail down the audience statement first?

Audience statement for Obsign:
My initial test audience would likely be mostly peers, such as those that I see in the office, or protocol-adjacent social media connections on Bluesky, and maybe some reach into the protocol-curious. After testing, the release audience I'd be looking to aim for the 1Password kind of audience, security-minded, or even not so technical folks who want to better their security hygiene. 

There is growing discussion on Bluesky about how users are *_NOT_* interested in concepts around "owning your data" among the most protocol-minded users. I'm not so sure myself, the truth is probably somewhere in the middle. However, I don't doubt the intelligence and insight of some of those making the argument, so it is something to keep in mind as well.


Audience statement for Custos:
Explicitly a technical-minded subset of Obsign users. Very few would be interested in owning the full stack, and the primary monetization angle would be on offering hosting tiers etc on the flagship Custos instance. These care deeply about how the technology works and wish to have the ultimate control over their data and presence on the network.

The audience statements change the plan in one important way: the release-audience Obsign user (1Password lane, security-minded, not necessarily technical) is who `user/` docs should be written for *now* — your test peers can read down, but a normie can't read up. And your note on the "owning your data" skepticism gives me a concrete framing rule: lead with what can go wrong and how Obsign protects you; let sovereignty be the outcome, not the pitch. Custos/operator docs keep their depth and just get the voice fixed.

# Writing Clearly and Concisely

## Overview

William Strunk Jr.'s *The Elements of Style* (1918) teaches you to write clearly and cut ruthlessly.

**WARNING:** `elements-of-style.md` consumes ~12,000 tokens. Read it only when writing or editing prose.

## When to Use This Skill

Use this skill whenever you write prose for humans:

- Documentation, README files, technical explanations
- Commit messages, pull request descriptions
- Error messages, UI copy, help text, comments
- Reports, summaries, or any explanation
- Editing to improve clarity

**If you're writing sentences for a human to read, use this skill.**

## Limited Context Strategy

When context is tight:
1. Write your draft using judgment
2. Dispatch a subagent with your draft and `elements-of-style.md`
3. Have the subagent copyedit and return the revision

## All Rules

### Elementary Rules of Usage (Grammar/Punctuation)
1. Form possessive singular by adding 's
2. Use comma after each term in series except last
3. Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas
4. Comma before conjunction introducing co-ordinate clause
5. Don't join independent clauses by comma
6. Don't break sentences in two
7. Participial phrase at beginning refers to grammatical subject

### Elementary Principles of Composition
8. One paragraph per topic
9. Begin paragraph with topic sentence
10. **Use active voice**
11. **Put statements in positive form**
12. **Use definite, specific, concrete language**
13. **Omit needless words**
14. Avoid succession of loose sentences
15. Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form
16. **Keep related words together**
17. Keep to one tense in summaries
18. **Place emphatic words at end of sentence**

### Section V: Words and Expressions Commonly Misused
Alphabetical reference for usage questions

## Bottom Line

Writing for humans? Read `elements-of-style.md` and apply the rules. Low on tokens? Dispatch a subagent to copyedit with the guide.

4	
5	Every night, an unattended Claude Code session wakes up, picks **one vertical

9	improves the *information* about that slice for both agent and human consumers.
10	A human reviews it over coffee in the morning.
11	
12	The name is deliberate: like sleep consolidating memory, the routine's job is
13	consolidation — finding stale claims, duplicated facts, missing connective
14	tissue, and confusing prose, and fixing them while the codebase is quiet. It
15	never changes behavior.
16	
17	## Why this exists
18	
19	The repo's deterministic gates (`just docs-check`, `bruno-check`,
20	`ticket-ref-check`, …) enforce *coverage* — every route has a reference entry,
21	no ticket refs leak into source. They cannot judge whether prose is still
22	*true*, whether three files state the same fact where one should be canonical,
23	or whether a comment narrates *what* instead of *why*. That is judgment work,
24	and it drifts silently as code moves. A nightly agent pass keeps the drift
25	bounded to about a day per vertical, and the PR-per-night shape keeps the human
26	cost to one small review.
27

29	[release-docs routine](release-docs-routine.md): the agent proposes, the
30	deterministic gates enforce the mechanical half, the human judges the prose.

33

35	   skips the night entirely rather than piling up review debt.

55	- **Information surfaces only.** Code comments, AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, `docs/`,
56	  Bruno request docs, `sites/docs` prose, conservative `sites/marketing`
57	  factual corrections, READMEs, doc comments. No renames, refactors,

64	- **No Linear writes.** Findings that deserve issues are listed in the PR body;
65	  the human promotes them. (Nightly automated issue-filing would spam the
66	  backlog, and headless sessions may not have the Linear connector anyway.)

71	## Configuring the Routine

73	The routine runs as a **cloud [Claude Code Routine](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/routines)**
74	with a **Schedule** trigger. Each firing spins up a **fresh, isolated cloud
75	session** — this file's spec is the whole memory, and no earlier conversation is

77	(or the Desktop app → **Routines** → **New routine** → **Remote**; **Local**
78	instead is a machine-bound Desktop scheduled task, the
79	[archive-sweep](scheduled-agents.md) pattern — not what this routine wants).

82	live spec**: editing the Routine prompt block below changes the next night's run
83	with no change to the routine's configuration. Paste this as the routine's
84	instructions:

88	docs/operations/dream-routine.md on origin/main and execute its "Routine prompt"
89	block verbatim, top to bottom, as tonight's run: preflight (skip the night if two
90	or more open "dream:" PRs exist), pick one vertical slice, investigate its full
91	stack, make information-only edits, run the cheap gates, and open a PR from a fresh
92	claude/dream/<date>-<slug> branch off origin/main. Use the GitHub connector to list
93	and open the PR. Keep your final report to the vertical chosen and the PR link, or
94	"dreamless night" plus what you checked.
95	```

100	  each run; the routine's own edits go on `claude/`-prefixed branches.
101	- **Environment:** the **Default** environment (**Trusted** network access) is
102	  enough — the run needs GitHub + Linear (both routed through Anthropic's
103	  connector channel, no allowlist entry required) and the default package
104	  registries for the `just` gates.
105	- **Trigger → Schedule:** **daily**, entered in your local timezone (a small
106	  fixed per-routine stagger may push the start a few minutes later). For an exact
107	  minute or a custom cron, save first, then `/schedule update` in the CLI (the
108	  minimum interval is one hour).
109	- **Connectors:** keep **GitHub** (needed to list/open the PR) and **Linear**
110	  (the routine reads Linear for context — e.g. checking whether a doc-fix is
111	  already tracked); remove connectors the run doesn't need.
112	- **Permissions:** leave **Allow unrestricted branch pushes** *off* — the routine
113	  only pushes `claude/dream/*` branches, already permitted by the default
114	  `claude/`-prefix rule.

116	Then **Create** and click **Run now** once to verify the first run can actually
117	push and open a PR before trusting the schedule.

119	**Two gotchas that bit the first setup (2026-07-17):**
120	
121	1. **Fresh sessions need connectors + repo attached.** A trigger created via the
122	   `create_trigger` MCP tool comes up *without* connector tools or push
123	   credentials — it can read the clone but cannot push or open a PR, defeating
124	   the whole deliverable. The claude.ai Routines UI (above) attaches both; the
125	   MCP-tool path does not. Always use the UI for this routine.
